Costa Rica has an overall safety risk rated as low. Violent crime is low and petty crime (pickpocketing, scams) is medium. The US State Department advises: Exercise Increased Caution. Exercise increased cautionin Costa Rica due to crime.
Petty crime is common throughout Costa Rica. Violent crime also affects tourists. This includes armed robbery, homicide, and sexual assault. For solo female travelers: Generally safe. Standard precautions apply. Avoid beaches at night alone. Catcalling is common but generally not threatening.. LGBTQ+ safety: Very LGBTQ+ friendly. Same-sex marriage legal since 2020. San José has a small but vibrant LGBTQ+ scene. Generally welcoming across the country.. Natural disaster risks include: earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, flooding, tropical storms.
In Costa Rica, call 911 for police, 911 for ambulance/medical emergency, and 911 for fire services.  The U.S. Embassy San José in San José can be reached at +506-2519-2000.

Costa Rica has a Mixed public/private (CAJA — Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social for residents; tourists can access both public and private). Private healthcare is excellent and affordable. healthcare system, rated good quality. Typical costs for tourists: System: Mixed public/private (CAJA — Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social for residents; tourists can access both public and private). Private healthcare is excellent and affordable. Quality: ★★★★☆ (4/5) Private healthcare in San José and major cities is excellent and affordable by US standards. Public hospitals (CCSS/CAJA) are available but often have long wait times. Many private doctors and specialists speak English. Pharmacies (farmacias) are widely available. Costa Rica is known for medical tourism. 💡 Medical Tourism Costa Rica is a well-known medical tourism destination, particularly for dental work, cosmetic surgery, and laser eye surgery. Costs are 40-70% lower than in the US. San José is the main hub with JCI-accredited hospitals. Popular for dental implants, crowns, veneers, and plastic surgery.. Pharmacy access: easy. Access: easy Hours: Most pharmacies open 8am-10pm; some 24-hour pharmacies in San José; chains include Fischel, Babel, and CVS pharmacies; many pharmacies have a 'pharmacy on call' system for after-hours Prescription rules: A Costa Rican prescription is technically required for prescription medications. Foreign prescriptions are not accepted. Some antibiotics and common drugs available OTC. Carry all medications in original packaging with a doctor's note. 💡 Tips Many medications available OTC. Pharmacists are helpful and often speak English. Bring a list with generic names. Some US brand names may not be available — bring alternatives. In rural areas, pharmacy selection is more limited. Recommended vaccinations: Hepatitis A, Hepatitis B, Typhoid (for extended stays or rural travel), Routine vaccinations (MMR, DTaP), COVID-19, Rabies (for animal exposure), Yellow Fever (required if arriving from yellow fever endemic countries; recommended for some areas). Malaria risk is negligible. Travel insurance advice: ⚠️ Strongly recommended Average cost: $25-50/week 💡 Tip Travel insurance is strongly recommended. Private healthcare is affordable ($50-200/doctor visit, $500-2,000/day hospital stay) but costs add up without insurance. Medical evacuation coverage is important for remote areas (Osa Peninsula, Monteverde, Caribbean coast). Ensure coverage includes adventure activities (zip-lining, surfing, etc.). 💡 Tip Travel insurance is strongly recommended. Private healthcare is affordable ($50-200/doctor visit, $500-2,000/day hospital stay) but costs add up without insurance. Medical evacuation coverage is important for remote areas (Osa Peninsula, Monteverde, Caribbean coast). Ensure coverage includes adventure activities (zip-lining, surfing, etc.).

Benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium) is restricted in Costa Rica. Controlled psychotropic substances under Costa Rican law. Available by prescription at pharmacies. Travelers should carry a doctor's letter and prescription.

Adderall / amphetamines is banned in Costa Rica. Amphetamines are prohibited substances. Adderall is not approved in Costa Rica. Importing may lead to legal complications. Carry extensive medical documentation if traveling with any stimulant medication.

Cannabis / CBD is caution in Costa Rica. Cannabis remains illegal for recreational use, but enforcement is relatively relaxed for small personal amounts. CBD derived from hemp is available in some shops. A 2022 bill legalized medical cannabis and hemp cultivation. Do not import cannabis products.
Methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta) is restricted in Costa Rica. Available by prescription. Carry valid prescription and original packaging. Costa Rica's pharmaceutical regulation is moderate.
Codeine / opioids is restricted in Costa Rica. Codeine combinations available by prescription. Stronger opioids require special controlled-substance prescriptions. Carry documentation.

Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) is restricted in Costa Rica. Regulated as a precursor chemical. Available in pharmacies with restrictions on quantity. Travelers can bring personal supply in original packaging.
Psilocybin / MDMA is banned in Costa Rica. Both are illegal under Costa Rican drug laws. Penalties for trafficking are severe. Despite the country's relaxed image, drug laws are enforced at borders.
Tramadol is restricted in Costa Rica. Prescription-only medication available at pharmacies. Carry prescription documentation.
Tranquilizers / sleeping pills (zolpidem) is restricted in Costa Rica. Prescription-only. Available locally. Carry doctor's letter and original packaging.

Mexico has an overall safety risk rated as medium. Violent crime is medium and petty crime (pickpocketing, scams) is high. The US State Department advises: Exercise Increased Caution. Exercise increased caution in Mexico due to terrorism, crime, and kidnapping.
Advisory summary

Many violent crimes take place in Mexico. They include homicide, kidnapping, carjacking, and robbery. There is a risk of terrorist violence, including terrorist attacks and other activity in Mexico. Visit the U.S. Department of State’s country reports on terrorism to learn more.  
The U.S. government has limited ability to help in many parts of Mexico. U.S. government employees are not allowed to trav For solo female travelers: Exercise increased caution. Tourist areas are generally safe during the day. Avoid traveling alone at night in unknown areas. Use Uber or official taxis. Femicide rates are high nationally — research specific areas carefully.. LGBTQ+ safety: Mexico City and Guadalajara are LGBTQ+ friendly with active scenes. Puerto Vallarta is one of Latin America's most LGBTQ+ welcoming resorts. Same-sex marriage legal nationwide. More conservative in rural areas.. Natural disaster risks include: earthquakes, hurricanes, tropical storms, volcanic activity (Popocatépetl).
In Mexico, call 911 for police, 911 for ambulance/medical emergency, and 911 for fire services.  The U.S. Embassy Mexico City in Mexico City can be reached at +52-55-5080-2000.

Mexico has a Mixed public-private system (IMSS for residents, ISSSTE for public employees). Tourists access private healthcare. healthcare system, rated moderate quality. Typical costs for tourists: System: Mixed public-private system (IMSS for residents, ISSSTE for public employees). Tourists access private healthcare. Quality: ★★★☆☆ (3/5) Private healthcare in major cities (Mexico City, Cancun, Puerto Vallarta) is good and affordable by US standards. Public hospitals can be overcrowded. Ensure you are treated at a reputable private facility. Medical tourism is popular for dental work and cosmetic surgery. 💡 Medical Tourism Mexico is a major medical tourism destination, especially for dental work, cosmetic surgery, and weight loss procedures. Costs are 50-70% lower than in the US.. Pharmacy access: very_easy. Access: very_easy Hours: Many pharmacies open 24/7, especially in tourist areas. Chain pharmacies like Farmacias Guadalajara, Benavides, and CVS are widely available. Prescription rules: Foreign prescriptions are generally not accepted for controlled substances. You may need a local Mexican prescription from a doctor. Report all medications to customs at entry. 💡 Tips Many medications that require prescriptions in the US are available OTC in Mexico, including antibiotics. However, it's still best to have a prescription. Keep medications in original packaging. Watch for counterfeit medications — buy from reputable chains. Recommended vaccinations: Hepatitis A, Hepatitis B, Typhoid (for extended travel or rural areas), Rabies (for animal contact), COVID-19 (following current guidelines). Malaria risk is present — consult a travel doctor before visiting. Travel insurance advice: ⚠️ Strongly recommended Average cost: $30-60/week 💡 Tip Purchase travel insurance that covers medical emergencies, hospitalization, and medical evacuation. Mexico's private hospitals expect payment upfront or guarantees from your insurance. Ensure your policy has a 24/7 assistance line in English. 💡 Tip Purchase travel insurance that covers medical emergencies, hospitalization, and medical evacuation. Mexico's private hospitals expect payment upfront or guarantees from your insurance. Ensure your policy has a 24/7 assistance line in English.

Benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium) is restricted in Mexico. Legal with prescription (receta médica). Classified under Fraction III of Mexico's General Health Law. Available at pharmacies with a valid prescription.

Adderall / amphetamines is banned in Mexico. Amphetamines are Fraction I controlled substances. Adderall is not approved or available in Mexico. Importing is illegal. Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) has limited availability with specialist prescription.

Cannabis / CBD is restricted in Mexico. Mexico's Supreme Court ruled recreational use constitutional (2021). Regulatory framework still pending full implementation. Medical cannabis and CBD products are legal with COFEPRIS authorization. Personal possession of ≤5g decriminalized.

Methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta) is restricted in Mexico. Available by prescription for ADHD (Fraction II psychotropic). Requires a special controlled substance prescription (receta especial). Carry original packaging and prescription.

Codeine / opioids is restricted in Mexico. Codeine combinations available with prescription. Stronger opioids require special prescriptions with COFEPRIS-regulated forms. Carry documentation for travel.
Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) is restricted in Mexico. Heavily regulated since 2008 due to methamphetamine production. Requires prescription and is tracked. OTC availability severely limited.

Psilocybin / MDMA is banned in Mexico. Both are illegal narcotics. However, traditional indigenous use of psilocybin mushrooms is culturally tolerated in certain regions (Oaxaca). No legal commercial availability.
Tramadol is restricted in Mexico. Available by prescription (Fraction IV). Standard medical prescription required. Widely available at pharmacies with valid Rx.

Tranquilizers / sleeping pills (zolpidem) is restricted in Mexico. Prescription required (Fraction IV psychotropic). Available at pharmacies with valid prescription. Carry documentation when traveling.

Scam alert in Acapulco, Mexico — Acapulco Guerrero-State Safety Context & 'Authentic Local Tour' Risk (tourist-trap, severity: high). Acapulco is in Guerrero state — under US State Department Level 4 'Do Not Travel' advisory due to cartel violence — and 2025 tourism has only partially recovered from Hurricane Otis (Cat 5, October 2023) which devastated the city. Traveler reports from 2025 consistently flag the US State Department Level 4 advisory, and travelers and Guerrero residents both express ongoing safety concerns in 2025 threads covering the broader Mexico safety baseline. The 2025 reality: (a) Acapulco's Diamante (south, newer) and Costera (Acapulco Bay strip) tourist zones are STATISTICALLY safer than the broader city — heavy police presence, well-patrolled, cruise-port active; (b) outer Acapulco neighborhoods (Renacimiento, Zapata, Acapulco Tradicional north) have elevated cartel-related risk and are NOT recommended for tourist visits; (c) Mexico City-Acapulco highway (the 'Autopista del Sol') has documented cartel checkpoints — NOT recommended as tourist drive; fly instead; (d) Taxco day-trip from Acapulco (4-hour drive each way) crosses risky rural Guerrero — go to Taxco from Mexico City instead; (e) 'authentic local Guerrero tour' offers via Instagram/WhatsApp targeting tourists for 'rural village experience' carry real cartel-zone risk; (f) Pie de la Cuesta / Coyuca lagoon day-trip is generally safe via licensed operator but risky via informal 'beach taxi' guide. For older travelers: (1) IF visiting Acapulco, stay in Diamante or Costera zones — avoid outer neighborhoods; (2) FLY between Mexico City and Acapulco — DO NOT drive the Autopista del Sol as a tourist; one-hour Aeromexico/VivaAerobus flights are MX$1,800-3,500; (3) for Taxco visit, go from Mexico City (3-hour drive on safer highways), NOT Acapulco; (4) REFUSE every 'authentic Guerrero village tour' Instagram/WhatsApp invitation; (5) check US State Department advisory before booking (travel.state.gov/Acapulco) — Level 4 is the highest US warning tier; (6) travel insurance with full evacuation coverage is essential for Guerrero; (7) save US Embassy 24-hr emergency +52 55 8526 2561; Mexican tourist police 911 (English available); (8) Hurricane Otis recovery context: many small businesses still rebuilding 2025 — verify hotel/restaurant operating status BEFORE booking via direct phone call. How to avoid: Stay in Diamante or Costera tourist zones only FLY Mexico City-Acapulco (Aeromexico/VivaAerobus MX$1,800-3,500) Visit Taxco from Mexico City (3-hour drive), NOT from Acapulco REFUSE every 'authentic Guerrero village' tour invitation Check travel.state.gov advisory; insurance with evacuation; US Embassy +52 55 8526 2561

Scam alert in Acapulco, Mexico — Acapulco Airport (ACA) & Cruise-Port Taxi Mafia Overcharge (transport, severity: high). Acapulco International Airport (ACA) and the cruise port have a documented 2025 taxi-overcharge ecosystem amplified by post-Hurricane Otis tourism scarcity (drivers hungry for fares). 2025 traveler reports cover the broader Acapulco-arrival landscape and safety context. Legitimate fares: ACA airport to Costera (15 km, 25 min) via official Transporte Terrestre prepaid MX$450-600; via Uber MX$300-450 (Uber works in Acapulco but supply is THIN — wait 10-20 min); to Diamante (12 km, 20 min) MX$350-500. Cruise pier to Costera MX$200-300 via taxi; to La Quebrada cliff divers MX$300-400. The 2025 scam patterns: (a) ACA arrivals-kerb kiosks quoting MX$1,200-2,500 for Costera transfer (2-5x real); (b) 'VIP private driver' at MX$3,500 for standard sedan; (c) 'security escort fee MX$300' added after the trip (no such legitimate fee); (d) Uber driver cancelling and re-quoting cash — same pattern as CDMX/Mazatlán; (e) cruise-pier 'authorized taxi' US$50-80 for trip that's MX$200-300 metered; (f) 'combined airport + cliff divers + sunset US$250 per person' bundle marked up 4x DIY cost; (g) 'Diamante private transfer with security US$200' upsells exploiting safety fears; (h) hotel concierge kickback directing to 'recommended driver' at 2x Uber rate. Traveler reports from 2025 confirm that hotel-arranged 'travel agency' tours are essentially always scam operations. For older travelers: (1) book Uber on airport Wi-Fi after luggage — typical ACA-Costera MX$300-450 (Uber works, 10-20 min wait); (2) alternatively official Transporte Terrestre prepaid booth inside arrivals MX$450-600 (legitimate flat-rate); (3) IGNORE every arrivals-kerb kiosk quoting MX$1,200+; (4) hotel airport pickup is the safest option — most Costera/Diamante hotels include free transfer with advance booking; (5) at cruise pier, use the OFFICIAL SECTUR taxi stand (rate posted) MX$200-300 to Costera; refuse 'private US$50' offers; (6) REFUSE 'security escort fee' and 'safety surcharge' demands — illegitimate; (7) for return to ACA, pre-book Uber or Transporte Terrestre night before; (8) save Acapulco Tourist Police +52 744 484 4583 (English available) and US Embassy +52 55 8526 2561. How to avoid: Book Uber on airport Wi-Fi: ACA-Costera MX$300-450 (10-20 min wait) Or Transporte Terrestre prepaid booth MX$450-600 Use hotel free airport pickup (most include with advance booking) Cruise pier: official SECTUR taxi MX$200-300 to Costera Tourist Police +52 744 484 4583; US Embassy +52 55 8526 2561

Scam alert in Acapulco, Mexico — La Quebrada Cliff Divers 'Premium View' & Photo Tout Scam (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Acapulco's La Quebrada cliff divers (clavadistas) — performing 35-meter dives into a narrow ocean inlet five times daily — is the city's iconic free public spectacle. The 2025 tout ecosystem around the show exploits tourists unfamiliar with the legitimate viewing options. Traveler reports from 2025 flag broader Acapulco tourism scams, and 2024 cruise-passenger reports cover Quebrada visits. Legitimate options: (a) FREE viewing from the public plaza (Mirador de la Quebrada) — best for the noon, 1 PM, and 7:30 PM dives; (b) El Mirador Hotel 'Coyuca 22' restaurant or 'La Perla' bar — order a drink/meal (MX$200-500) and watch from the terrace with the best angle; (c) 'official' clavadistas plaza ticket MX$50-80 for guaranteed seating during the 9:30 PM torch dive (the most spectacular). The total visit cost should be MX$50-200 per person. The 2025 scam patterns: (a) 'premium VIP viewing area MX$500 per person' touts at the plaza approach — no such VIP area exists at the public viewpoint; (b) 'photographer with telephoto for the dive' service quoting MX$300-800 then delivering blurry phone-photo (real professional photos are sold by the divers' association at MX$100); (c) 'private terrace reservation US$100 per person' at La Perla bar (a drink + view is MX$200 at the bar); (d) 'cliff diver meet & greet MX$400' (divers post-show take free tips MX$30-50 — no formal 'meet & greet' fee exists); (e) 'sunset cliff dive special show MX$1,000' — the 7:30 PM dive is one of the regular five daily, free to view from plaza; (f) bundled cruise-day 'Quebrada VIP + hotel transfer US$120' marking up MX$300 actual cost. For older travelers: (1) for the 7:30 PM or 9:30 PM dive, arrive 30-45 min early to get a good spot at the public plaza viewpoint (FREE); (2) for guaranteed seating, the 9:30 PM torch dive plaza ticket is MX$50-80 (sold at the gate); (3) for the BEST view, order a drink at La Perla bar (Hotel El Mirador) — MX$200 buys you a margarita and the terrace view; (4) REFUSE every 'VIP viewing area MX$500', 'private photographer MX$300', 'meet & greet MX$400' offer — none is legitimate; (5) tip individual divers post-show MX$30-50 if you want to thank them; (6) cliff-diver photographs available at the divers' association booth MX$80-100; (7) the divers' show times (varies seasonally): 1 PM, 7:30 PM, 8:30 PM, 9:30 PM, 10:30 PM — verify on quebradacliffsdivers.com; (8) Quebrada is in Old Acapulco — well-policed during show hours but take Uber back to hotel after dark. How to avoid: Arrive 30-45 min early at FREE public plaza for 7:30/9:30 PM dive Or 9:30 PM torch dive plaza ticket MX$50-80 at gate for guaranteed seat Best view: order MX$200 margarita at La Perla bar (Hotel El Mirador) REFUSE 'VIP viewing', 'private photographer', 'meet & greet' upsells Tip divers post-show MX$30-50; photos at association booth MX$80-100

Scam alert in Acapulco, Mexico — Acapulco Diamante Resort Timeshare & 'Hurricane-Recovery' Pressure Sale (tourist-trap, severity: high). Acapulco's Diamante and Costera resort sectors host a 2025 timeshare-presentation ecosystem with a unique post-Hurricane-Otis 'rebuilding investment' angle. Traveler reports from 2025 flag hotel-pitch scams, and the US State Department Level 4 advisory context makes 'investment in Acapulco' pitches especially risky. The 2025 scam patterns: (a) Diamante resort welcome desks (Princess Mundo Imperial, Vidanta Acapulco) offering 'free breakfast + US$200 credit + Diamante access' for '90-min preview'; (b) 'Acapulco rebuilding investment opportunity US$25,000+' pitched as patriotic post-Otis recovery (high-risk speculative); (c) 'fractional ownership rental yield 8-12% guaranteed' — no rental yield can be guaranteed in a USDOS Level 4 destination; (d) high-pressure 3-5 hour presentations with closer escalation; (e) 'snowbird membership US$15,000-30,000' targeting US/Canadian retirees; (f) 'cancellation fee US$500' to exit early; (g) 'celebrity endorser' name-drop tactics (Hurricane Otis recovery features prominently in pitches); (h) 'Mexican real estate fideicomiso required US$5,000 admin fee' — fideicomiso IS the legal structure for foreigner property in Mexico's restricted coastal zone, but admin fees are normally MX$10,000-25,000 (US$600-1,500), not US$5,000. For older travelers: (1) JUST SAY NO at Diamante / Costera resort welcome desks — 'free breakfast + credit' offers are timeshare pitches in disguise; (2) IF attending, set 90-min HARD STOP and stand to leave regardless of tactics; (3) NEVER authorize credit-card 'holds' or 'deposits' during presentation; (4) Mexican 5-business-day cooling-off period is LAW — file PROFECO (profeco.gob.mx) + registered mail to property's legal department within window if you signed; (5) CRITICAL: 'Acapulco rebuilding investment' is high-risk speculative — Hurricane Otis (Cat 5, October 2023) destroyed huge infrastructure; recovery is ongoing; cartel-violence safety overlay makes Acapulco real estate a poor investment for casual buyers; (6) for genuine Mexican property, consult a LICENSED Mexican real-estate attorney (NOT the resort's 'legal counsel') with verifiable Notario Público; (7) REFUSE any 'fideicomiso admin US$5,000' — real range is US$600-1,500; (8) US Consulate Acapulco closed 2024 — nearest US Consulate is Mexico City Embassy +52 55 8526 2561; (9) traveler reports from 2025 confirm that 'travel agencies' approaching at hotel are essentially always timeshare-pitch organizations. How to avoid: JUST SAY NO at Diamante / Costera resort welcome desks If attending, 90-min hard stop; stand and walk out regardless of tactics NEVER authorize credit-card 'holds' or 'deposits' Mexican 5-day cooling-off: file PROFECO if signed For property, consult licensed Mexican real-estate attorney; refuse 'investment' speculation

Scam alert in Acapulco, Mexico — Acapulco Costera Restaurant Tourist-Menu & 'Mariscos Market Price' Padding (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Acapulco's Costera Miguel Alemán beachfront restaurant strip and Diamante mall dining hosts a 2025 tourist-menu bill-padding ecosystem common to Mexican beach destinations. Traveler reports from 2025 cover the broader Acapulco scam landscape, and 2024 cruise-day reports document dining patterns. The 2025 scam patterns: (a) Costera beachfront restaurants with USD-only menus at 2-3x local prices (huachinango fish dish US$30+ vs MX$200-300 at working-class spots); (b) 'mariscos market price' verbal quotes for shrimp/lobster/fish without weight × price/kg disclosed — bills run MX$1,500-3,500; (c) 'gratuity 18%' pre-added + tip line (double-tipping); (d) 'credit-card processing 10-15%' announced at bill; (e) 'complimentary chips/guacamole' arriving as MX$280 line item; (f) 'fresh coconut water US$8' from beach-vendor at restaurant when fair MX$30-50; (g) USD-priced menus padding 10-15% exchange; (h) 'live mariachi service charge MX$100/person' added unannounced; (i) 'special seafood platter market price' that's whatever they decide to charge; (j) Acapulco Old-town zócalo restaurants charging Diamante prices to cruise tourists. For older travelers: (1) eat at AUTHENTIC Acapulco spots: La Cabaña de Caleta (Caleta beach, Mexican seafood, Google 4.6+, MX$250-450), El Cabrito (Costera, traditional Mexican, MX$200-400), 100% Natural (Costera multi-locations, healthier MX$150-300), Becco al Mare (Costera Italian, transparent MX$300-500 per person); (2) for shrimp/seafood, agree weight × price/kg IN WRITING before cooking — fair shrimp MX$400-600/kg, lobster MX$1,000-1,500/kg, fish MX$200-400/kg depending on type; (3) INSPECT bill — refuse 'gratuity 18% + tip' double-dipping; confirm card surcharge 0-3% BEFORE ordering; (4) request MX$ bill (not USD); (5) REFUSE uninvited 'complimentary' appetizers (always charged); (6) for budget eats, Mercado Central de Acapulco (Old Acapulco) has authentic seafood at MX$80-150 per meal; (7) refuse 'live mariachi service charge' — if you want music, agree per-song MX$100-200 with the musicians directly; (8) coconut water from beach vendor: MX$30-50 fair (NEVER US$8 in MX$ pesos). How to avoid: Authentic: La Cabaña de Caleta, El Cabrito, 100% Natural, Becco al Mare Seafood: weight × price/kg IN WRITING; fair shrimp MX$400-600/kg Inspect bill; refuse double-tipping; card 0-3% Mercado Central de Acapulco for budget MX$80-150 Mariachi: agree per-song MX$100-200 with musicians directly

Scam alert in Acapulco, Mexico — Acapulco Beach Vendor & 'Free Massage' Aggressive Pressure Scam (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Acapulco's public beaches host an active 2025 vendor culture with aggressive pressure tactics. Scam alert in Isla Mujeres, Mexico — Isla Mujeres Garrafón / Punta Sur Park Entry & 'Mandatory Guide' Fee Padding (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Scam alert in Jacó, Costa Rica — Jacó Nightlife Drink-Spiking & 'Costa Rican Friend' Robbery Setup (theft, severity: high). Jacó is the most-documented drink-spiking destination in Costa Rica's Central Pacific. The Tico Times 2025 'Danger In Costa Rica? Rising Crime' coverage names Jacó as the darkest node on the rising-crime map: 'Jacó is a drug town taken by all sorts of shady people.' The 2025 pattern runs on Avenida Pastor Díaz nightlife — Beatle Bar, Le Loft, Orange Pub — and especially Hotel Cocal & Casino's pool bar, which TripAdvisor (187+ reviews) describes as 'prostitutes and thieves,' with one reviewer robbed of '$2k and my passport while I was out fishing.' Traveler reports gathered the definitive field advice: 'Watch your drink, have the bartender open the beer in sight'; 'Your largest safety concern is the people you will let in the room — their mission is to steal your wallet/phone/key card. Also, if you have a payment dispute, their male friends will be very effective in collections'; 'lots of post clients belongings disappearing even out of the hotel room safes.' The pattern: a tourist buys drinks for a friendly 'Costa Rican friend' or a woman at the bar; a benzodiazepine or scopolamine (burundanga) drop goes into the unattended bottle; within 20–40 minutes the victim is disoriented and walks back to the room with the 'friend'; accomplices enter, empty the safe (often with the drugged victim's cooperation), and leave. Locals are blunt: 'Jaco is a place for gringos looking for sex … lots of prostitution and drugs … brings security issues of all kinds.'

For travelers hitting Jacó nightlife, the playbook: (1) order only bottled/canned drinks and watch the bartender open them — never accept a drink from a 'new friend' or dancer; (2) if you leave a drink to use the restroom, abandon it and order fresh; (3) avoid Hotel Cocal & Casino entirely for lodging — the pool bar is a documented theft zone and in-room safe theft is repeatedly reported; safer: Hotel Club del Mar, Crocs Resort (family side), DoCe Lunas, or Los Sueños condos; (4) never bring a Jacó-bar companion back to your room — the accomplice-for-collections pattern is consistent across three years of reports; (5) if you feel sudden dissociation or slurred speech 20–40 min after a drink, walk to a lit restaurant and call 911 — the 9-1-1 Tourist Police Operations Center launched Sept 2025 has English dispatch; keep your passport in the lobby safe-deposit box (not the in-room safe, compromised at Cocal), and carry only a color-copy + one card to the strip. How to avoid: Bottled/canned drinks only, opened in front of you — never accept from a stranger. Never bring a Jacó nightlife companion back to your hotel room. Avoid Hotel Cocal lodging; safer: Club del Mar, Crocs Resort, DoCe Lunas, Los Sueños. Passport in lobby safe-deposit box (not in-room safe); carry only color-copy to bars. If drugged symptoms hit: walk to a lit restaurant, call 911 (new tourist-police center, 2025).

Scam alert in Jacó, Costa Rica — 'Costa Joe' — Named WhatsApp/Facebook Fixer Deposit Fraud (Cars, Golf Carts, Airbnbs) (accommodation, severity: high). He will pretend to get you set with car, car rentals, Airbnbs, rides, golf carts, and anything else he can promise and try to get you to pay a deposit. Then when it's time to deliver, he ghosts. Been scamming for quite a while. He's probably early to mid-20's, WhatsApp is his preferred method of communication.' The Facebook 'Playas del Coco' group post 'Scam Alert: Beware of Joseph Goodwin and Costa Joe in Car Deals' confirms the real name and extends the racket to Coco/Guanacaste. Named-victim testimony includes: 'Joseph Goodwin. He sold me a messed up car claiming all good. Looks like I got lucky since I actually got a car, another lady paid and got ghosted'; 'Yes, Costa Joe is well known on some Facebook groups. Many people have been ripped off by him'; 'Already reported his number as a scam in TrueCaller.' The racket is classic advance-fee: a $200–$800 USD deposit via SINPE Móvil, WhatsApp-linked transfer, Zelle, or crypto for a car rental, golf cart, Airbnb, fishing charter, or jetski; after payment the address produces no car and no answer. Sock-puppet FB accounts tag each other with fake 'great guy, rented from him twice' endorsements to build social proof.

For travelers planning a Jacó rental in 2025/2026, the playbook: (1) book cars only through major chains — Adobe Rent-a-Car, Budget, Economy, Alamo, National — at SJO airport pickup in person; never WhatsApp handoff; average $45–$100/day with insurance disclosed at counter; (2) golf carts: rent only at physical Avenida Pastor Díaz storefronts (JacoLuxe, AXR Jaco, Adventure Tours CR) — never from Facebook; 2025 rates $80–$120/day, deposits $200–$300 on card; (3) refuse all WhatsApp/Facebook deposit requests from individuals, even if 'recommended' — sock puppets are the mechanism; (4) Airbnbs only through Airbnb platform payment — never 'partly cash on arrival' or 'Zelle me a deposit'; (5) fishing/jetski: licensed ICT-registered operators only (Pacific Jungle Adventures, Maverick Sportfishing, R Sport Fishing); (6) if you've paid Costa Joe, email OIJ fraud (oij_fraudes@poder-judicial.go.cr), file credit-card chargeback within 60 days; travelers also recommend contacting Trivision, Central Noticias, or Multimedios 'to put pressure on the bureaucrats to do something.' How to avoid: Cars: only major chains at SJO counter (Adobe, Budget, Alamo, National, Economy). Golf carts: Avenida Pastor Díaz physical storefronts (JacoLuxe, AXR Jaco) — card deposit. Airbnbs: Airbnb platform payment only — refuse any 'cash on arrival' request. Charters/jetski: licensed ICT-registered operators (Pacific Jungle Adventures, Maverick, R Sport Fishing). If scammed: OIJ fraud email oij_fraudes@poder-judicial.go.cr + credit-card chargeback within 60 days.

Scam alert in Jacó, Costa Rica — Jacó Beach Parking Fake 'No-Park Zone' Reflective-Vest Extortion (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Travelers describe the mechanism: 'If you are parking in Jaco beach area there is a scam there where they will rope your car off and say you parked in a no park zone when you didn't. They wear a reflective vest and it all seems real … they'll ask for a random amount of $.' The scam exploits Costa Rica's informal 'guachiman' (from English 'watchman') culture where unofficial attendants legitimately work Jacó beach lots in yellow vests and expect a ₡500–₡2,000 (~$1–$4) tip. The scam inverts it: men in identical vests rope off a legal spot with cones or caution tape, wait for a tourist to park, then demand '$20 or I call the tow truck.' Traveler reports extend the pattern to organized break-ins at the Jaco Walk plaza lot specifically — 'the parking guard was in on it': the 'attendant' is casing the vehicle and signaling accomplices with an RF key-jammer that blocks the fob lock signal so your car flashes but doesn't lock. Travelers also flagged the vehicle-specific pattern: 'The jimny car seems like the main target for this type of robbery, they know its a rental car and tourists often travel with all of their belongings in the car.' Coordination has been reported at Jaco Walk, Hotel Cocal lot, and the main Playa Jacó beach strip.

For travelers parking in Jacó in 2025/2026, the playbook: (1) use hotel or restaurant parking over street parking — Jaco Walk interior, Crocs Resort lot, and Los Sueños marina lots have CCTV; (2) if you must street-park, legitimate guachimen accept ₡500–₡1,000 (~$1–$2) tip on return — anyone demanding $10–$20 upfront is running the scam; (3) never pay a 'fine' in cash to a reflective-vested man claiming a no-park zone — demand municipal paperwork (Boleta Municipal de Tránsito, stamped); (4) double-check your car is actually locked after the fob press — pull the handle manually; the key-jammer trick is widespread at Central Pacific beach lots; (5) never leave passports, laptops, cameras, or daypacks visible — hide them in the trunk before arriving at the lot (thieves watch the transfer); (6) if extorted or threatened, note the vest number, photograph the scene, and report to Jacó Tourist Police substation or OIJ Jacó subdelegación on Avenida Pastor Díaz, or call 911 (English dispatch via the new Tourist Police Operations Center, launched Sept 2025). How to avoid: Park at hotel/restaurant lots with CCTV (Jaco Walk interior, Crocs Resort, Los Sueños). Legitimate guachiman tip: ₡500–₡1,000 on return — never a fixed dollar amount upfront. Pull the door handle manually after locking — defeat key-jammer trick. Hide all valuables in trunk before arriving at the lot (never during transfer). Report extortion: OIJ Jacó subdelegación Avenida Pastor Díaz, or call 911.

Scam alert in Jacó, Costa Rica — Monteverde/Jacó Tours CR Copycat-Domain Booking Fraud (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Traveler reports document the SEO-based copycat-domain fraud that has been draining deposits from Jacó- and Monteverde-bound travelers since at least 2023. Another traveler noted: 'When this company started they directly copied the name of well known respected company called Monteverde Tours (the only change was they added CR to their email).' The same domain farm books Jacó-side day-tours (Carara crocodile boat, Catarata Bijagual, Jacó zipline combos). One traveler wrote: 'They canceled the tour because the water levels were too high. 2 months now, they've promised to refund me. Going through CapitalOne to get my money back.' For travelers booking Jacó-area tours in 2025/2026, the playbook: (1) never prepay more than a $50–$100 deposit — legitimate operators (Jacó Tours, Adventure Tours CR, Pacific Jungle Adventures) accept balance on arrival in cash or card; (2) book through buyer-protected marketplaces — Viator, GetYourGuide, Expedia Tours, or TripAdvisor Experiences — which refund when operators cancel; (3) verify the operator's TripAdvisor listing before paying; if no TripAdvisor/Viator link on the operator's own site, that's the red flag; (4) pay credit card only (Visa/Mastercard) — never wire, SINPE, Zelle, crypto; chargeback via issuer is the only reliable recovery (travelers report money came back via Chase fraud investigation); (5) cross-reference on Google — monteverdetours.com (since 2002) vs monteverdetourscr.com (scam); similar copycats exist for 'Jaco Tours' and 'Arenal Tours'; (6) if scammed, file credit-card dispute within 60 days and report to Defensoría del Consumidor at consumidor.go.cr. How to avoid: Never prepay more than $50–$100 deposit — balance on arrival, always. Book via Viator / GetYourGuide / TripAdvisor Experiences with platform refund protection. Verify legitimate domain: monteverdetours.com (since 2002), NOT monteverdetourscr.com. Pay credit card only — no wire / SINPE / Zelle / crypto for tour deposits. If scammed: credit-card chargeback within 60 days + consumidor.go.cr complaint.

Scam alert in Jacó, Costa Rica — SJO↔Jacó 'Private Shuttle' & Taxi Overcharge at Arrivals (transport, severity: moderate). Jacó sits 96 km (1 hr 45 min) southwest of SJO on Route 27, and the transfer is the most over-quoted tourist run in Costa Rica. Traveler reports establish the 2024/2025 baseline: 'Taxi is around $120. Pura vida rides advertises $109 (WhatsApp +506 7189-3268). I've heard didi is cheaper.' Travelers confirm: '$70, from downtown, on a Monday morning. No issues' and '$140 is pretty normal for a private shuttle to Jaco. You could probably get an uber slightly cheaper if there are fewer than 3 in your party.' The budget option: San Jose–Jaco public bus at $6–$8 cash, every 2 hours from downtown Terminal 7-10 (not the airport — a short Uber from SJO). The scam: tourists at SJO arrivals are approached by men waving 'Shuttle Jacó' signs quoting $200–$300 for a run that legitimately costs $120 by metered taxi, $70–$100 Uber/DiDi, or $50–$65/person via Interbus shared shuttle. Related: unverified 'driver' numbers from Facebook groups demand USD prepayment via Zelle/Venmo, then either no-show or demand second cash payment claiming the prepayment 'didn't go through.' One traveler noted: 'My Airbnb hosts in San Jose offered me rides that were 40 to 133 percent more than Uber.' Another long-time resident summarized: 'as someone who had been a resident of Costa Rica for 17 years, taxi drivers will always try to charge you excessive fares specially.'

For travelers arriving at SJO bound for Jacó in 2025/2026, the playbook: (1) Uber works at SJO for Jacó — $70–$100 typical, app-paid, transparent; walk to the designated rideshare pickup zone and screenshot the fare on arrivals-hall WiFi before exiting; (2) licensed metered red taxi (Taxi Aeropuerto, orange-and-yellow only — NOT random white cars) runs $100–$130 flat with receipt — never accept from an arrivals-hall tout; (3) Interbus (interbusonline.com) shared shuttle SJO–Jacó runs ~$50–$65/person, door-to-door, prepay by card on the site; (4) Tracopa/Quepos public bus from downtown San José is $6–$8 cash every 2 hours, requires a $10–$15 Uber from SJO to the terminal first; (5) never pay a WhatsApp 'driver' via Zelle/Venmo/SINPE before pickup — legitimate operators accept card on platform or cash-on-arrival only; (6) for pre-booked private transfer, use verified platforms (Viator, SJO Shuttle, Interbus.com, Two Weeks in Costa Rica) at $180–$215 private van rather than a random WhatsApp contact. How to avoid: Uber from SJO to Jacó — $70–$100, app-paid, screenshot fare inside terminal first. Licensed Taxi Aeropuerto (orange-and-yellow): ~$100–$130 with receipt. Interbus shared shuttle: ~$50–$65/person, prepaid on interbusonline.com. Cheapest: Tracopa bus from downtown Terminal 7-10 ($6–$8) via $10 Uber from SJO. Verified private pre-booking via Viator / SJO Shuttle / Two Weeks in Costa Rica.

Scam alert in Jacó, Costa Rica — Jacó ATV & Golf Cart Rental Damage-Inflation Deposit Trap (accommodation, severity: moderate). Jacó is Costa Rica's ATV and golf-cart rental capital, with legitimate and scam operators side-by-side on Avenida Pastor Díaz. 2025/2026 prices at reputable storefronts (AXR Jaco, Adventure Tours CR, Aventuras AVT Rentals, JacoLuxe): ATV 2-hour ~$90, half-day (4h) $150, full-day (8h) $200, 24-hour $250; golf cart $80–$120/day with $200–$300 credit-card-hold. One traveler noted: 'Our car rental deposit was released within 24 hours. The ATV deposit took almost a week. It wasn't a big deal...' — delayed releases are the norm, not the scam. The scam comes from two sides: (1) Costa-Joe WhatsApp fixers demanding cash deposits for a 'golf cart that will be delivered'; (2) Front-office damage-inflation — the vehicle passes pre-rental with only generic scratches noted, then on return staff 'discovers' a new scratch, 'cracked fender,' 'worn tires,' or 'mud damage' and bills $300–$800. Traveler reports note: 'How did u guys pay the deposit? These are the payment options I got from them on whatsapp and none seem a good option' — sketchy operators request SINPE Móvil transfers to personal accounts rather than card at the counter. Travelers catalog the pattern: 'lowball car rentals are the bait, and high insurance or $2700 to $20000 deposits if [damage found].' The pattern extends to Jacó ATVs/golf carts — smaller deposit, same inflation tactic.

For travelers renting ATVs or golf carts in Jacó in 2025/2026, the playbook: (1) rent only from Avenida Pastor Díaz storefronts with Google Maps presence — AXR Jaco, Aventuras AVT Rentals, JacoLuxe, Adventure Tours CR; never from WhatsApp-only 'fixers'; (2) pre-rental walkaround is non-negotiable — take a date-stamped 360° video (not photos) including tires, fender undersides, engine compartment BEFORE leaving the lot; narrate defects into the mic; save to cloud; (3) inspection sheet must list EVERY existing defect before you sign — if they refuse or list 'general scratches,' walk away; (4) pay deposit by credit card (Visa/Mastercard) — never cash or SINPE Móvil — so you have chargeback power; a $200–$300 card hold is legitimate, a $500+ cash demand is not; (5) 2025 rates: ATV $90/2hr, $150 half-day, $200 full-day, $250 24hr; golf cart $80–$120/day with $200–$300 card hold; anything far below is bait; (6) at return, joint walkaround + fresh video; refuse to sign 'damage acknowledged' without seeing pre-rental video; dispute fraudulent charges via card and Defensoría del Consumidor (consumidor.go.cr). How to avoid: Rent only from Avenida Pastor Díaz storefronts: AXR Jaco, Aventuras AVT, JacoLuxe, Adventure Tours CR. Date-stamped video walkaround BEFORE leaving lot — narrate defects, save to cloud. Inspection sheet must list every existing defect — walk away if vague. Deposit by credit card (card hold $200–$300) — never cash or SINPE. Return: joint walkaround + fresh video; dispute any fabricated damage via card issuer.

Scam alert in Jacó, Costa Rica — Jacó Mirador & Beach Opportunistic Robbery / Belongings Theft (theft, severity: high). The Mirador Jacó (abandoned villa viewpoint above south Jacó with graffiti and Pacific views) is the most-named specific robbery hotspot in Jacó. One traveler wrote: 'Stay away from the Mirador Jaco - tourists get robbed there all day, every day.' Counter-voices report uneventful midday visits — the risk cluster is late afternoon, evening, solo walkers, and visible camera gear. Combined with beach theft on Playa Jacó, travelers report: 'unattended phones and wallets disappear quickly.' Traveler reports surface adjacent Playa Hermosa beach-parking theft: 'Yep same thing happened to my Jimny earlier this month near Uvita' with passenger door pried and iPhone gone. Another traveler summarized: 'Property crime is the biggest issue in CR for visitors. Car break-ins, AirBnB burglaries, theft of belongings left unattended on the beach.' The Tico Times 'Danger in Costa Rica? Rising Crime' names Jacó; travelers add: 'Tamarindo has become Jacó but more expensive. Thanks to the drug market.' The Jacó beach pattern: a tourist leaves phone/wallet/daypack on a towel; a walker lifts the bag while they're 30m offshore; the walker blends into Avenida Pastor Díaz within 90 seconds. Mirador variant: 2–3 men approach a solo hiker near the villa, ask for the time/directions, demand phone and wallet.

For travelers at Jacó beaches and the Mirador in 2025/2026, the playbook: (1) never hike the Mirador Jacó solo — groups of 3+, daylight only, before 4 PM; the trail is short (~30 min up) but the isolated villa area is where approaches happen; (2) on Playa Jacó, carry only what fits in a waterproof neck-pouch (phone, one card, $20 cash, hotel key) — everything else in the hotel safe; (3) use a dry-bag phone pouch in the water rather than a towel on sand; (4) at Playa Hermosa surf break (5 km south), park at Backyard Bar/Hotel lot ($5 attended) rather than roadside — surf-bag theft at roadside is documented; (5) after sunset do NOT walk the beach — risk ranking: beach-at-night > Mirador > parking-lot > Avenida Pastor Díaz > hotel-room; travelers note: 'The risk on beaches at night is robbery and theft'; (6) if robbed: no resistance, hand items over, walk to a lit restaurant, call 911 (new 2025 Tourist Police Operations Center with English dispatch); report to OIJ Jacó subdelegación on Avenida Pastor Díaz within 24h for insurance claim. How to avoid: Mirador Jacó: groups of 3+, daylight only, never after 4 PM. Beach: waterproof neck-pouch for phone/card/$20/key — rest in hotel safe. Playa Hermosa: park at attended Backyard Bar/Hotel lot ($5), never roadside. Never walk Jacó beach after sunset — beach-at-night is the top risk. If robbed: no resistance, call 911, OIJ Jacó on Avenida Pastor Díaz within 24h.

Scam alert in La Fortuna, Costa Rica — Lava Land Tours 'Sloth Tour' Bait-and-Switch — Julio's Downtown Storefront (tourist-trap, severity: high). A named-operator PSA still surfaces as the top SerpAPI result for 'La Fortuna scam' in 2025/2026. The owner's name is Julio; the public WhatsApp/phone is +506 8442 7337. One traveler paid $160 USD cash for a 'sloth tour at a nature preserve with an English-speaking guide.' What happened: Julio's employee led the group to a private villa where an older Costa Rican man with binoculars — no English, no sloths — walked '500 m in front of us' through rainforest. Using Google Translate they discovered there was no actual guide, just the binocular-holder. Back at the desk, Julio refused to refund, shouted profanities on the main street, and 'booked a hot spring' substitute they later discovered cost $10, not $160. The traveler noted: 'I went on TripAdvisor and this is pretty standard for this company.' The same pattern appears in Facebook La Fortuna scam posts: 'Adventure Arenal Travel Agency' / Pedro Antonio Badilla Berrocal (cash-only Rio Celeste tour, no tour delivered, refund refused); and Google Reviews for 'Horseback Riding Costa Rica La Fortuna' document identical deposit-taken / tour-never-happened waterfall-horseback scams. Traveler reports from 2024 document the same storefront-commission archetype with 'Tour Operators Costa Rica' / Alon.

For travelers booking La Fortuna tours in 2025/2026: (1) never book at a cash-only downtown storefront without verifying ICT (Instituto Costarricense de Turismo) registration at visitcostarica.com's business directory — unregistered operators have no recourse path; (2) book directly with the source — Rio Celeste Ranger Station, La Fortuna Waterfall ADIFORT ($18 at the gate), Mistico Hanging Bridges on-site; (3) credit card only (Visa/Mastercard/Amex) — disputable within 120 days; cash, Zelle, or PayPal 'friends & family' = no recourse; (4) 2025 traveler-recommended operators: Desafio Adventure Costa Rica (desafiocostarica.com, 25+ years, ICT-certified), Eco Terra Costa Rica, Canoa Aventura — or book through hotel front desk (one traveler noted 'Always had my best luck booking tours through our hotels'); (5) cross-check TripAdvisor AND Google Reviews same day — a 4.9 TA with <40 reviews + 2.1 Google is a rebrand; (6) if scammed: ICT consumer line via visitcostarica.com/en/contact-us, consumidor.go.cr, and card-issuer dispute within 60 days; OIJ fraud line 800-8000-645; US Embassy San José +506 2519-2000. How to avoid: Verify ICT-registered operators at visitcostarica.com business directory. Book Desafio Adventure, Eco Terra Costa Rica, Canoa Aventura, or hotel front desk only. Credit card payment only — disputable within 120 days (Visa/Mastercard/Amex). Cross-check TripAdvisor + Google Reviews same day; rebrand scams show inconsistency. Report: ICT via visitcostarica.com, consumidor.go.cr, US Embassy +506 2519-2000, OIJ 800-8000-645.

Scam alert in La Fortuna, Costa Rica — La Fortuna Red Taxi Meter 'María' Tampering & Inflated Excursion-Meetup Fares (transport, severity: moderate). A first-person traveler report anchors the pattern. Scenario: the traveler's Uber ghosted (car didn't move for 10 min on app), the hotel called a red taxi; within the first minute the meter ('María') was already at ₡8,000; at the 15-min arrival it hit ₡17,500 (~$35). The driver produced a calculator and subtracted ₡6,000 to 'make it right' at ~$23 — still roughly 2x the Uber estimate of $10. One traveler noted: 'Official taxis here scam everyone, local or not, as long as you look kind of lost. It happened to me when I first started living in San [José]' — clarifying meters don't start at zero but at a regulated ₡700–₡900 base. Others confirm legitimate 2024 per-km rates of roughly $2/km (the national MOPT-regulated rate is ₡645 base + ₡640/km in 2025, per costa-rica-guide.com and costaricatravelblog.com). Scam variants: (1) María hot-wired to tick 2–3x regulation — a 5 km trip that should show ₡3,200 shows ₡8,000+; (2) 'meter broken' + verbal flat rate 2–3x legit; (3) detour around La Fortuna's one-way loop adds 1–2 km; (4) LED flicker defeats phone cameras (the traveler's photo captured nothing) so driver quotes a verbal figure higher than what briefly showed; (5) fake 'Sunday tariff' or 'holiday tariff' — Costa Rica does have a Tarifa 2 with 20% uplift after 10 PM and Sundays, but never during weekday daytime. La Fortuna's compact layout (Parque La Fortuna → most hotels within 3 km, most trail access within 8 km) means legitimate in-town fares are ₡2,500–₡6,000 (~$5–$12); anything $15+ inside town is a scam.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) use Uber or DiDi exclusively — both operate in La Fortuna (Uber more reliable, DiDi backup); typical La Fortuna→Arenal 1968 trailhead Uber $8–$14 vs red taxi $25–$35; (2) if red taxi: say 'con María' (meter on) BEFORE the car moves; watch the base start ₡650–₡900, never higher; (3) video-record the meter at start AND end (defeats LED flicker); (4) correct 2025 rate ₡645 base + ₡640/km + ₡645 per 6-min stuck-in-traffic; sub-10 km in-town trips shouldn't exceed ₡7,500 (~$14); (5) pay credit card or SINPE Móvil where accepted — never hand over ₡20,000 or $50 bills; (6) complaint: Consejo de Transporte Público 2523-2000 or ctp.go.cr with the dashboard yellow-triangle ID number; (7) SJO→La Fortuna transfer alternatives: Interbus shared shuttle $56–$75, private shuttle $140–$200 for 1–4 pax, Sansa Air $89 to the small Fortuna airstrip when running. How to avoid: Uber / DiDi exclusively — $8–$14 typical vs red taxi $25–$35. If red taxi: say 'con María' before car moves; confirm base starts ₡650–₡900. Video-record meter start AND end (defeats LED flicker). Expect ₡645 base + ₡640/km — under ₡7,500 (~$14) for sub-10 km trips. Complaint: Consejo de Transporte Público 2523-2000 / ctp.go.cr with dashboard ID number.

Scam alert in La Fortuna, Costa Rica — Roadside 'Private Hot Springs' Booth Scam — Fake Day-Pass Collectors Near Rio Chollín (street-scam, severity: moderate). Rio Chollín (also Choyín / El Chollín) is La Fortuna's legitimately FREE natural hot-spring river — a warm tributary flowing from Tabacón Thermal Resort's upstream source under the Route 142 bridge, legal to visit 24/7 at zero cost. But because it sits immediately adjacent to Tabacón ($99 day pass), Baldi ($51–$99), Paradise ($64), and Titoku ($52), roadside operators have set up fake 'parking + entrance' booths that look like official hot-springs tickets. Walkmyworld.com's 2025 guide 'El Choyin: Read this before visiting' explicitly warns about the 'parking mafia' near the pullout. Mechanics: (1) men in reflective vests wave cars to a 'parking' area 200 m before the real pullout, charge $5–$10 for 'hot springs day access' which is free; (2) a roadside table with 'Hot Springs Parking — $8' and attendants claiming the pullout is 'their lot'; (3) more aggressive operators follow the group to the river and demand 'entrance fee' at the water's edge — there is no entrance fee, it's a public watercourse; (4) slashed-tire intimidation for cars that refuse (per costaricatravelblog.com's 2025 Rio Chollín guide). Related: some downtown La Fortuna tour operators sell a '$30 private hot springs day tour' that is actually just the free Rio Chollín — driver drops you off, pockets the fee. Tabacón, Baldi, Paradise, Titoku, and EcoTermales are the legitimate commercial resorts; their 2025/2026 day passes range $51–$99 with clear signed gates, never roadside booths.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) Rio Chollín / El Chollín / El Choyín is FREE — no legitimate fee exists; drive Route 142 toward Nuevo Arenal, cross the Tabacón bridge at ~8 km from La Fortuna, and park in the free pullout on the right 100 m past the bridge — NOT at any manned 'parking' booth before the bridge; (2) daylight only — costaricatravelblog.com's 2025 guide warns the free springs are 'not safe after dark' (theft + flash-flood risk); (3) valuables in hotel safe; waterproof dry bag with minimal cash + phone + key; (4) never pay any attended 'parking' booth on the approach — there are no legitimate paid lots for Rio Chollín; (5) 2025/2026 paid spring prices: Tabacón $99 day pass, Baldi $51 / $75 (meal) / $99 (two meals), Paradise $64 w/meal, Titoku $52 w/meal, EcoTermales $50 reservation only; (6) book paid resort passes direct from the resort website — downtown 'combo deals' add 25–40% commission and sometimes just resell the free Rio Chollín; (7) if a roadside 'attendant' blocks you, drive on — report to Fuerza Pública La Fortuna 2479-9288 or 911. How to avoid: Know Rio Chollín / El Chollín is FREE — park in the pullout past the Tabacón bridge only. Daylight hours only; waterproof dry bag with minimal cash + phone + key. For paid springs: Tabacón $99, Baldi $51, Paradise $64, Titoku $52, EcoTermales $50. Book paid resort passes direct — not via downtown '25% commission' combos. Report roadside blockers: Fuerza Pública La Fortuna 2479-9288 or 911.

Scam alert in La Fortuna, Costa Rica — La Fortuna Waterfall 'Unofficial Parking Permit' Collectors at ADIFORT Gate (tourist-trap, severity: low). La Fortuna Waterfall (Catarata La Fortuna), managed by ADIFORT (Asociación de Desarrollo Integral de La Fortuna), charges an official $18 USD entrance fee in 2026 — card only, no cash, per confirmed Instagram and tripadvisor.com 2025/2026 reporting; $20 is the recent prior rate. Parking is INCLUDED in the ticket — no separate charge at the real gate. But on the 1 km approach road, roadside collectors in reflective vests and sometimes khaki uniforms charge fake 'parking permits' of $3–$10 before the gate, passing themselves off as ADIFORT staff. Traveler reports confirm: 'Had the same thing happen just outside La Fortuna' — the Manuel Antonio Route-618 template has migrated to the Waterfall access road. The Mytanfeet.com 2025 guide notes: 'The entrance fee is $20 USD for foreigners ages 9 and up. Parking is free at the official lot.' Mechanics: (1) vest-wearers stop cars 500 m before the gate, charge $5 'parking' that doesn't exist; (2) a 'guide' materializes to walk you the 530 steps down (not needed — stairs are concrete with handrails); (3) cash-only fake 'entrance tickets' for $15–$20 that don't work at the real ADIFORT turnstile (card-only per 2026 reports). Traveler reports confirm: the Waterfall, Rio Chollín, Arenal 1968 trail, and Mistico Hanging Bridges are all self-drivable with clearly signed official gates that take cards; no roadside intermediary is necessary or legitimate.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) drive to the actual ADIFORT gate at the end of the access road — the real ticket office is a permanent concrete building with ADIFORT signage, turnstiles, card readers, and uniformed staff; (2) legitimate 2026 fee: $18 adult, $5 child 5–11, free under 5 — card only, no cash; (3) parking at the official lot is INCLUDED in entry — anyone charging separate 'parking' on the approach is a scammer; (4) hours 8 AM–5 PM daily, last entry ~3:30 PM; arrive 8–9 AM for fewest people and better swimming at the base per Instagram 2025 guides; (5) sturdy grip shoes for the 530-step descent; 'official guide' pressure at the entrance is unnecessary (single path, handrails); (6) if blocked by a roadside 'permit' collector, drive past — photograph the person and spot, report to Fuerza Pública La Fortuna 2479-9288 or to ADIFORT staff at the gate; (7) bring dry bag, change of clothes, water shoes, biodegradable sunscreen — normal sunscreen is prohibited in the base swimming zone. How to avoid: Drive to the actual ADIFORT gate — concrete building, card readers, turnstiles, uniformed staff. Legitimate entry: $18 adult / $5 child 5–11 / free under 5 (card only, no cash). Official parking INCLUDED in entry fee — never pay separately on the approach. Arrive 8–9 AM; wear grip shoes, bring dry bag + water shoes + biodegradable sunscreen. Report fake collectors: Fuerza Pública La Fortuna 2479-9288 or report at real ADIFORT gate.

Scam alert in La Fortuna, Costa Rica — Jeep-Boat-Jeep Monteverde Shuttle — Double-Booking & Luggage-Weight 'Overage' Fees (transport, severity: moderate). The 'Jeep-Boat-Jeep' (sometimes 'Taxi-Boat-Taxi') is La Fortuna's signature 3-hour crossing to Monteverde: a 4×4 van from La Fortuna hotels to Arenal Lake, a 25-minute boat across the lake, then another 4×4 up the unpaved road to Monteverde/Santa Elena. It's like transport and a tour rolled into one'). Traveler reports confirm the legitimate route is 'easy, affordable, quick, and fun' at $27–$35 pp — scam variants target tourists booking at downtown commission offices rather than direct.

For travelers crossing Arenal–Monteverde in 2025/2026: (1) book direct with Desafio Adventure (desafiocostarica.com), Jacamar Tours, Vamos Rent-a-Car's transfer desk, or hotel front desk — never via a downtown cold-sell office; $25–$35 pp one-way; (2) email confirmation BEFORE paying: pickup hotel + time, total price (no legit operator charges luggage separately), arrival hotel + ETA, refund policy; (3) credit card only — disputable if service isn't delivered; (4) pickup 6:30–8:00 AM, Monteverde arrival 11:00 AM–12:30 PM; 'running 2 hours late' = double-booked scam, demand refund or hold the card charge; (5) keep laptop/passport/phone/cash in a personal daypack; checked luggage rides on top of jeep or in boat hold; (6) the boat crossing is 25 min — request a window seat for volcano photos; life jackets provided and required; (7) mobility alternative: private La Fortuna–Monteverde shuttle $180–$240 via Interbus for 1–4 pax, door-to-door, no boat — useful during Oct–Nov heavy rain. How to avoid: Book direct: Desafio Adventure, Jacamar Tours, or hotel front desk ($25–$35 pp). Email confirmation: pickup hotel + time + total price + arrival + refund policy. Credit card only — disputable if not delivered. Keep laptop/passport/phone in personal daypack; never in checked luggage. If weather/mobility issue: private shuttle $180–$240 via Interbus 1–4 pax, no boat.

Scam alert in La Fortuna, Costa Rica — Arenal Backpackers / Societal La Fortuna — Hostel Listing-vs-Reality & Third-Party Booking Freeze-Out (street-scam, severity: moderate). Two documented patterns target budget travelers in La Fortuna. (1) Listing-vs-Reality: one traveler described booking an $83 'private room' at Arenal Backpackers Resort, arrived to find 'a bed inside a concrete tube with no floor space, only space for you to walk in and walk out.' No refund despite checking out immediately. Commenters recommend Lomas del Volcán as a fair-priced alternative, and Palacios Arenal as a legitimate budget option. (2) Third-Party Freeze-Out: one traveler booked Societal La Fortuna via Expedia for $550 CAD, arrived after a long bus day to be told the hotel 'had local-government issues and couldn't host them'; the hotel claimed to have emailed (guests never received), Expedia claimed no notifications reached them either. The traveler was out $550 CAD and paid again for Yay Arenal Waterfall Lodge. Expedia spent 5 days failing to reach the hotel, then denied the refund because 'they couldn't get ahold of anyone.' One commenter put it bluntly: 'They sold you something and they are fully aware that you did not receive it. But still refuse a refund? It's cut and dry.' Others advise credit-card chargeback — which bypasses Expedia's 'we tried' defense. Mechanics: (i) misleading listing photos — the Arenal Backpackers 'concrete tube' bears no resemblance to the listing; (ii) hotel license or tax issues cause last-minute cancellations never passed to the OTA; (iii) third-party OTA acts as a buffer preventing direct accountability; (iv) 'cash deposit on arrival' adds a second loss layer.

For travelers booking La Fortuna lodging in 2025/2026: (1) book direct from the hotel website where possible — get owner name, email, Tax ID (cédula jurídica) in the confirmation; community-recommended: Lomas del Volcán ($100–$150 volcano-view cabins), Arenal Observatory Lodge ($165+), Volcano Lodge ($130–$200), Hotel Magic Mountain, Palacios Arenal Hostel (budget); (2) if using third-party, stick to Expedia, Booking.com, or Hostelworld — never Facebook Marketplace or WhatsApp; read the 5 most-recent <3-star reviews for current problems; (3) save listing photos + reservation PDF before travel as chargeback evidence; (4) 24–48h pre-arrival, confirm with the hotel directly by email AND phone — no response = re-book + open chargeback; (5) credit card only (Visa/MC/Amex/Cap One) — Amex and Cap One Travel Protection handle OTA disputes well; (6) stranded on arrival: same-day rebook Lomas del Volcán / Arenal Observatory / Palacios Arenal walk-in; file Expedia/Booking complaint + card chargeback within 60 days; also consumidor.go.cr; (7) for hostels, read the Hostelworld 'private room' text description carefully — 'capsule,' 'compact,' or '10 m²' are red flags for the Arenal Backpackers 'concrete tube' phenomenon. How to avoid: Book direct via hotel website with cédula jurídica + owner name + email on record. La Fortuna recommended: Lomas del Volcán, Arenal Observatory Lodge, Volcano Lodge, Palacios Arenal. Always use credit card (Visa/MC/Amex/Cap One) — chargeback within 60 days. Read the 5 most-recent <3-star reviews; photograph listing images before travel. Confirm reservation 24–48h pre-arrival by email + phone; if stranded, Booking.com walk-in + chargeback.

Scam alert in La Fortuna, Costa Rica — La Fortuna Vrbo / Vacation-Rental Inside Job — Last-Night Power-Cut Electronics Theft (accommodation, severity: high). A high-stakes vacation-rental inside job has been widely documented in traveler reports. On the guests' last night they went to dinner; returned to find laptops, headphones, phones, cash, watches, and more missing. House was locked, TV still playing Netflix, no sign of forced entry. Host's explanation: 'they shut the power off for 15 minutes' — but the TV was still running Netflix from before they left, and the thieves left the TV. Stolen devices pinged moving toward San Ramón; last known location was a San Ramón bus stop. The traveler noted later: 'The police (with language barrier) indicated that this place has been hit before' and 'someone messaged me and said they stayed at the same property and got robbed this year.' Community commenters noted similar patterns: 'Can you link the property? I want to move to LF one day and would like to bookmark this place'; 'If you have renter's insurance back home, be sure to file claims. I lost my wedding ring in Mexico and got 75% reimbursed'; others cross-referenced Vrbo and identified two matching listings, one 'Premier Host' with volcano views and pool. Mechanics: (1) 'Premier Host' / 'Superhost' status is no safeguard — platforms award on volume + minimum ratings, not integrity checks; (2) isolated villa = no neighbors watching; (3) the 'dinner on last night' pattern is highly predictable and timed by host or accomplice; (4) pre-planned cover story ('power cut'); (5) Find My / Google Find My Device reveal rapid movement to San Ramón within hours.

For travelers booking La Fortuna rentals in 2025/2026: (1) avoid remote isolated villas in the El Castillo / Chachagua / El Tanque corridor — prefer in-town apartments or established hotels; (2) before booking, read every 1- and 2-star Vrbo/Airbnb review — one 'electronics stolen' note is a dealbreaker; cross-reference host name on Google + TripAdvisor; (3) on your LAST NIGHT (highest-risk per traveler reports), take laptops + passports + jewelry + cash to dinner OR transfer to your next hotel if moving on; (4) pre-trip: enable Find My iPhone / Google Find My Device on every device with email + phone alerts ON — you get notified if devices move during dinner; (5) report theft IMMEDIATELY: Fuerza Pública La Fortuna 2479-9288 + OIJ 800-8000-645; get a denuncia (police report) copy — required for travel insurance and Vrbo/Airbnb claims; (6) file Vrbo Host Damage / Airbnb Resolution Center claim within 14 days; (7) US homeowners/renters insurance (USAA, Amica, State Farm, Liberty Mutual) typically covers off-premises theft at 10–20% of dwelling coverage; credit-card travel insurance (Chase Sapphire Reserve, Amex Platinum) covers up to $3,000 in stolen personal effects; (8) email trust-safety@vrbo.com with the denuncia — pattern theft eventually triggers delisting. How to avoid: Prefer in-town La Fortuna apartments or hotels over isolated El Castillo/Chachagua villas. Last night: take laptops/passports/jewelry/cash to dinner OR transfer to next hotel. Enable Find My iPhone / Find My Device with email + phone alerts pre-trip. Report theft: Fuerza Pública La Fortuna 2479-9288 + OIJ 800-8000-645 for denuncia. Credit-card travel insurance (Chase Sapphire Reserve / Amex Platinum) covers up to $3k stolen effects.

Scam alert in Liberia, Costa Rica — Avis LIR 'Mandatory Insurance' Bait-and-Switch — $123 Online Becomes $444 at the Counter (financial-fraud, severity: high). Avis at Liberia airport has the worst community reputation of any single rental branch in Costa Rica — a named repeat offender across three separate 2025/2026 PSA threads. One traveler wrote: 'We reserved a car through hertz to pick up at Liberia airport. Online reservation total was $123. By the time we left the rental office that had ballooned to $444.' Another traveler noted: 'We paid $350 online for our car rental that "included" liability and they charged us another $350 for liability when we arrived.' A 2026 traveler was blunt: 'Avis Liberia airport is a highly fraudulent and scamming location, they prey on tourists big time... staff and owners are all heavily involved and will use your credit card the way they want.' One commenter added: 'Hertz Liberia did this to us too. Same scam. False damage claims, we even had photo & video proof the damage existed at pickup.' A January 2026 traveler reported: 'Our insurance covered rental car and yet we had to buy insurance that cost more than the rental car... Brought the car back early due a flat tire... $300.'

Key distinction: Costa Rican law requires only Third-Party Liability (TPL/SLI), ₡5,000–₡5,500/day (~$10–$11), covering injuries to other people. Everything else — Collision Damage Waiver, Theft, Supplemental Liability — is optional and covered by many US credit cards (Chase Sapphire, Amex Platinum, Capital One Venture X). One community explainer: 'The law says the only required insurance from the companies is the third party liability... NOT REQUIRED is any collision damage coverage.' The bait works because online quotes hide even mandatory TPL, so a $10/day rental discovers $30–$60/day of 'mandatory' insurance at pickup.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) skip Avis, Hertz, Budget, Fox, Europcar at LIR — community consensus: 'Vamos or Adobe, or take your chances. Hertz, Avis etc are unreliable here'; (2) book direct at adobecar.com (MyTanFeet $25 off) or vamosrentacar.com (10% cash discount) — both ICT-licensed, 4.5+ Google, all-in pricing; (3) bring a PRINTED Costa Rica-specific CDW letter from Chase / Amex / Capital One or pay $25–$60/day; (4) only TPL/SLI ~$10–$11/day is required — decline all else in writing; (5) photograph every angle including spare (community tip: 'Check the spare too. Rip off companies') and odometer; (6) budget $2,000+ credit-card room for deposit hold; (7) if Avis/Hertz LIR refuses your CDW letter, walk away and rebook Adobe/Vamos in the same terminal; (8) file ICT complaint 2299-5800 and credit-card chargeback. How to avoid: Book Adobe (adobecar.com + MyTanFeet $25 off) or Vamos (vamosrentacar.com, cash 10% off) — skip Avis/Hertz/Budget/Fox at LIR. Bring PRINTED Costa Rica-specific CDW letter from Chase Sapphire / Amex / Capital One Venture X. Pay only mandatory TPL/SLI at ~$10–$11/day; decline all other insurance in writing. Photograph every angle of car + spare + odometer on pickup and return; flag all scratches on contract. File ICT complaint at 2299-5800 and credit-card chargeback if Avis/Hertz tries false damage claims.

Scam alert in Liberia, Costa Rica — Budget / Hertz / Fox / Europcar LIR Counter Phantom-Fee Stack — $800 Rental Becomes $1,800 (accommodation, severity: high). Interestingly the US Alamo site was $300 cheaper than the Alamo.cr site. We paid $1,380 for 16 days.' That traveler booked via the US Alamo site. How to avoid: Book DIRECT with Adobe, Vamos, or Sun Valley — skip Economybookings, Priceline, Hotwire aggregators.
