For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) book MEPE directly at the Gran Terminal del Caribe ticket window or via email reservation — $12–$13 seated, seniors ~₡1,000 off with passport; (2) for door-to-door, book only at caribeshuttle.com ($54 PV–SJO), interbusonline.com, or via your hotel's concierge; (3) avoid Viator / GetYourGuide resellers — 30% markup; direct is always cheaper; (4) arrive 15 minutes early at MEPE, carry ₡10,000 for fare + ~₡1,000 per checked bag; (5) NEVER buy a shuttle ticket from a Calle 217 hustler — go to the Caribe Shuttle office at Calle 213 & Ave 69 (next to Flip Flop Store) or book online; (6) solo traveler with heavy luggage? Private Interbus ($120) or Arenal Rides (traveler-recommended) is worth it; (7) confirm an email reservation number day-of — phantom bookings are the #1 red flag. How to avoid: MEPE: buy directly at Gran Terminal del Caribe (Calle Central, Av 11) window, ₡5,960–₡6,760 cash. Shuttle: book only at caribeshuttle.com ($54) or interbusonline.com; hotel concierge acceptable. Arrive 15 minutes early at MEPE window; carry ₡1,000 per checked bag. Avoid Viator / GetYourGuide resellers — 30% markup; use the operator's own website. Confirm every shuttle has an email confirmation + QR; no confirmation = phantom booking.

Scam alert in Puerto Viejo, Costa Rica — Airbnb / Villa Inside-Job Burglary during Advertised 'Power Outage' — Playa Cocles and Punta Uva Rentals (accommodation, severity: moderate). The inside-job burglary is the Caribbean's most financially damaging residential scam because most Puerto Viejo rentals have no on-site security and are managed by a single caretaker / housekeeper who has a key copy, your itinerary, and knows which drawer holds your cash. Mechanic: the caretaker commits the burglary or tips off an accomplice, framed as a 'power outage' (to disable battery-backup cameras) that conveniently occurs the night you announce a Manzanillo dinner. September 2024 and January 2026 traveler reports document the pattern: guests return from a beach dinner to find the unit ransacked, the power out, no forced entry, and the caretaker 'heartbroken' on their behalf.

An October 2025 traveler thread noted the Caribbean hostels are 'very removed from Limón,' but that isolation means single-caretaker rentals with no backup. A January 2025 Pacific-side report referenced the parallel pattern: 'They do this to keyless start cars, as well as your rooms you are staying in while you are out.' The February 2026 Kurt Van Dyke home-invasion murder in Cahuita elevated the profile of acquaintance-driven crime in the region. Burglary values: typically $2,000–$8,000 per incident — laptops, cameras, cash, passports, jewelry.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) rent ONLY properties with on-site staff — boutique options include La Costa de Papito (Playa Cocles), Azania Bungalows, Shawandha Lodge (Playa Chiquita), Selvin's Cabinas (Punta Uva), or Cariblue Beach & Jungle Resort; caretaker-only villas are high-risk; (2) read every Airbnb / VRBO review for the phrases 'power was out,' 'felt watched,' or 'left us a note about when we'd be home' — all canaries; (3) use a Pacsafe Travelsafe 12L ($60) locked to the bed frame for passports, cash, and electronics; (4) never tell the caretaker your daily plans — vague 'we'll be out' only; (5) install a Wyze or Ring mini-camera with cellular cloud backup facing the entry; (6) leave lights on timers and a radio playing; (7) buy travel insurance with theft coverage — Allianz Global, World Nomads, or Chase Sapphire Reserve's rider — and document serial numbers of all electronics in advance. How to avoid: Book boutique hotels with 24/7 front desk: La Costa de Papito, Azania, Shawandha, Selvin's, Cariblue. Use a Pacsafe Travelsafe 12L ($60) locked to bed frame for passports, cash, electronics. Never share your daily plans with the caretaker — vague answers only. Install a Wyze or Ring mini-camera with cellular cloud backup facing the entry door. Carry theft-covered travel insurance (Allianz Global, World Nomads) + document all serials in advance.

Scam alert in San Cristobal de las Casas, Mexico — San Juan Chamula & Zinacantán Indigenous Village Tour Commission Scam (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). San Juan Chamula and Zinacantán are indigenous Tzotzil Maya communities 10-20 km from San Cristóbal — culturally significant but sensitive (sacred church rituals, shamanistic practices). The 2025 tour ecosystem hosts commission-kickback and cultural-insensitivity scams. Independent visit: colectivo from San Cristóbal MX$30-50 each way, church entry MX$50. Zinacantán textile workshops: free to visit, fair prices MX$500-2,500 for hand-loomed goods. The 2025 scam patterns: (a) San Cristóbal tour kiosks selling 'private Chamula + Zinacantán tour US$150 per person' (real small-group MX$400-800); (b) 'exclusive shaman ceremony US$100 per person' — shamanistic rituals at Chamula church are SACRED, NOT tourist performances (attempting to participate is culturally offensive); (c) 'Zinacantán weaver's cooperative' shops marking up 3-5x at commission-rate via tour-bus drivers; (d) 'photography permit MX$500' at Chamula church (NO photography is allowed inside — this is cultural taboo, NOT a fee); (e) 'mandatory Mayan blessing MX$300' by fake shamans approaching tourists; (f) 'combined Chamula + Zinacantán + cenote US$200' that eats the whole day; (g) 'Mezcal Posh tasting US$40' where Posh (Tzotzil ritual alcohol) is MX$80-120 per bottle at the village. For older travelers and cultural-respect: (1) book SMALL-GROUP tours ONLY via Google 4.7+ operators with cultural-sensitivity credentials: Alex & Raul Jaramillo Tours, Marvinjaime Tours, César Tours — MX$400-800 per person half-day; (2) CRITICAL: NO PHOTOGRAPHY inside San Juan Chamula church (cultural taboo, can result in confiscation of equipment or worse); photograph only exterior; (3) REFUSE every 'shaman ceremony' or 'Mayan blessing' offer — authentic rituals are NOT performed for tourists; attempting to participate is culturally offensive; (4) at Zinacantán, buy textiles at fair prices: rebozos MX$800-2,000, blouses MX$500-1,500, rugs MX$1,500-4,000 — ask to see weaver workshop rather than 'cooperative shop'; (5) church entry at Chamula is MX$50 (pay at entrance) — no 'photography permit' exists (photography is forbidden); (6) dress respectfully (covered shoulders + knees) and remove hat inside church; (7) Posh (Tzotzil ritual drink) is traditional — fair MX$80-120 per bottle, not US$40 per tasting. How to avoid: Book reputable cultural-sensitivity operators: Alex & Raul Jaramillo, Marvinjaime NO PHOTOGRAPHY inside Chamula church (cultural taboo) REFUSE 'shaman ceremony' / 'Mayan blessing' offers Zinacantán textiles: rebozos MX$800-2,000, blouses MX$500-1,500 Church entry MX$50 at entrance; no 'photography permit' exists

Scam alert in San Cristobal de las Casas, Mexico — Palenque Ruins Day-Trip Unlicensed Operator & 'Mandatory Guide' Scam (tourist-trap, severity: high). How to avoid: Book Google 4.7+ operators: Explora Chiapas, Kukulcán, Chiapas Selva Lacandona Consider 2-day overnight version (MX$2,500-4,000) for older travelers Palenque official entry: MX$130 total; NO mandatory guide Agua Azul MX$80 at gate; Misol-Ha MX$25 Refuse 'mandatory guide', 'VIP', 'skip-line' claims

Adelina Flores) — direct-from-farmer transparent pricing MX$180-400 per kg; (4) for Mezcal Posh, buy at El Paliacate Mezcaleria (authentic Chiapas mezcal) or travel to village for direct-from-producer MX$80-200; (5) REFUSE 'authentic cooperative' claims without verifiable Sna Jolobil or Jolom Mayaetik certification; (6) Mercado de Dulces y Artesanías has general goods at fair prices but verify each item; (7) genuine Zapatista-community goods: look for specific cooperative labels (Tzotik cooperative, Yaxalum); (8) silver: verify .925 hallmark STAMPED into metal (not sticker); Taxco-style silver is not Chiapan (Chiapan has distinct amber-focused jewelry); (9) traveler reports maintain a verified shop list. Scam alert in San Jose, Costa Rica — SJO Airport Pirate-Taxi Cartel — $40 for a 4-Minute Ride & Worse (transport, severity: high). SJO's official airport-taxi system is a monopoly concession run by Taxi Aeropuerto — cars are ORANGE (not the city's red), plates start with 'T' (TA, TSJ, TH, TP, TG), and the fare is fixed at a KIOSK INSIDE the terminal before you walk to the cab. Anyone outside the terminal quoting $20–$150 in a non-orange car is a pirata. An August 2025 traveler report describes the violent end: 'A gang of taxi drivers is targeting foreigners in San José. They offer cheap fares, then meet accomplices along the route, assault passengers, steal everything, and dump them on the street.' Another traveler: '$40 in a taxi to get 5 minutes from the airport. Driver gave us an insane price and when I called him out on it, he basically acknowledged it and said there's nothing I could do but pay.' A November 2024 traveler report documents the near-kidnap: the traveler and husband arrived late at SJO, 'lady from the group came over and took our bags and guided us to a red taxi'; 20 minutes later they realized they were on the highway going the wrong way toward 'meeting people who were going to rob us.' A native Tico commenter clarified: 'Official taxis always start with T — TSJ, TA, TH, TP, TG + numbers. Regular private plates are six numbers or XXX 999.' The fake-Uber variant is documented separately. In a February 2024 traveler report, the traveler's driver dropped them at SJO, sped off WITHOUT ending the fare, drove loops, ended at ₡20,000 instead of the ₡3,900 quoted — a 5x gouge.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) at arrivals IGNORE every 'taxi taxi' shout and anyone reaching for your bag — as one traveler put it: 'if somebody unexpectedly picks up your bags… most likely going to lead to a scam or possibly something worse'; (2) walk to the Taxi Aeropuerto orange-kiosk IN the terminal (not the curb) — fare is ~$28–$33 to central San José / Paseo Colón, ~$40 to Escazú, ~$12–$18 to Alajuela hotels — and walk to the numbered orange cab they assign; (3) photograph the plate (must start with 'T') + driver's ID card BEFORE loading luggage; (4) alternative: pre-booked Interbus/Gray Line shuttle ($15–$25 pp shared) or hotel car (Intercontinental, Marriott Hacienda Belén offer free/paid shuttles); (5) Uber is often cheaper (travelers report ₡10,000 SJO → Hotel Continental ≈ $19) BUT gray-legal at SJO — sit up front to avoid airport-police notice, VERIFY driver ENDS the trip before you exit (travelers report '$200 fraudulent driver charge fixed only after Uber dispute'); (6) screenshot Uber quoted fare + pickup time; dispute any >2x overage with credit-card chargeback; (7) NEVER accept a 'shared' ride at an unofficial curb pickup — the highway-shakedown pattern; emergency 911, US Embassy 2519-2000, OIJ 800-8000-645. How to avoid: Pay at the Taxi Aeropuerto orange kiosk INSIDE the SJO terminal (~$28–$40 fixed). Verify plate starts with 'T' + photograph driver's ID + plate before loading bags. If Uber: sit up front, confirm driver ENDS the trip in app before you exit the vehicle. Pre-book Interbus/Gray Line ($15–$25 pp) or hotel shuttle as safest 1 AM option. Never accept a stranger's grab for your luggage — force them to put it down.

Scam alert in San Jose, Costa Rica — Fake Uber at SJO + Driver-Doesn't-End-Trip Fare Gouge (transport, severity: moderate). Uber operates in Costa Rica (since 2015) but has never been formally legalized — the ARESEP transport regulator still officially considers rideshare illegal, and airport-taxi concessionaires actively police it at SJO. This grey zone creates two scam surfaces. First, the 'fake Uber' — a pirate-taxi driver stands at arrivals with a sign showing the rider's name (pulled from a social-media leak), and peels the tourist off the real Uber. October 2025 and 2026 traveler reports both document the 'driver cancels, friend-cousin-with-a-van steps in' pattern. Second, the 'driver doesn't end the fare' gouge: a February 2024 traveler report shows a traveler paid ₡3,900 quoted, driver dropped them at SJO, sped off WITHOUT ending the ride, drove loops, ended at ₡20,000 — a 5x gouge. Another commenter advised: 'Threaten Uber with a chargeback. Your credit card company will easily refund that.' One traveler reports an Arenal surge version — quoted ₡2,300, ended ₡9,800. Another in Liberia: '$9 ride → $30 charge, over 16 km beyond actual drop-off,' refunded only after credit-card dispute. Third, the 'express kidnapping' tail: an October 2025 traveler report documents a driver who exited at drop-off, physically restrained the traveler, went through their pockets, took $130 cash. A 2020 traveler report sums the Tico view: 'At the airport take the orange taxis and everywhere else, just use Uber.' Another traveler: 'A friend paid about $200 for a ride because of a fraudulent driver (Uber refunded it).'

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) when booking Uber at SJO meet the driver on the UPPER/DEPARTURES level (travelers advise: 'find stairs up to go to departures, and the Uber will pick you up there') — airport police enforce against Uber at arrivals but not departures; (2) VERIFY the in-app plate matches the physical plate exactly; (3) ask the driver 'cuál es mi nombre?' — if they can't name you, it's a fake Uber; (4) at drop-off DO NOT EXIT until the driver taps 'End trip' and the receipt email arrives — if they speed off, screenshot the open trip and call Uber support immediately; (5) screenshot the quoted fare before the ride starts — proof for Uber and credit-card chargeback (Capital One, Chase Sapphire, Amex Platinum handle this well); (6) prefer DiDi (travelers note: 'same software, operates throughout Latin America') or InDrive as cheaper gray-legal alternatives; (7) late-night solo travelers should prefer orange taxi or hotel shuttle over Uber at that hour — most respondents on a 2024 traveler thread flagged the 1 AM SJO airport Uber experience as risk-heavy. How to avoid: Meet Uber on the SJO DEPARTURES level (upstairs) not arrivals — escapes airport-police ban. Verify in-app plate MATCHES physical plate + ask 'cuál es mi nombre?' before entering. Watch driver 'End Trip' in the app + receipt email arrive before exiting the vehicle. Screenshot quoted fare + route in app; dispute overages with Uber + credit-card chargeback. Prefer DiDi or InDrive at equivalent prices; late-night solo: orange taxi or hotel shuttle.

Scam alert in San Jose, Costa Rica — Claro / Kolbi SIM-Card 'Activation Fee' Fraud at SJO Baggage Claim (financial-fraud, severity: low). A May 2023 traveler report captures the canonical write-up: 'Whatever you do, do NOT buy a local simcard at the Claro stand where you collect your bags in SJO airport. These guys are a fraud. They only accept cash and do not give change. They cannot give a receipt. They offer Claro's MOST EXPENSIVE pre-paid card as the "cheapest" pre-paid plan they have. The simcard you receive works for a couple of hours after which it gets blocked.' Follow-up: 'When we went to a Claro shop in San Jose the next day they told us the sim cards were not activated and thus we paid for nothing… and we needed to pay again.' One commenter noted a legit counter-example; the original traveler clarified: 'Presumably the Claro shop employees do really sell the genuine thing… but from time to time they freeload on ignorant tourists like myself and keep the money for themselves.' Mechanics: real Claro/Kolbi prepaid SIMs with 5GB run ~₡5,000–₡10,000 (~$10–$20) at any in-city Claro or Kolbi store; the airport kiosk charges $25–$45 CASH ONLY, no receipt, sells an 'activated' SIM that dies after 2 hours, pockets the difference. A parallel TripAdvisor thread 'Scammed in Tamarindo Purchasing a SIM card' documents the same vendor network at beach kiosks. Legitimate 2025/2026 alternatives: Airalo eSIM (bought before flight, activates on landing, $4.50–$17 for 1–10GB, runs on Liberty/Claro); Kolbi SIM at Multiplaza Escazú, Mall San Pedro, or a Walmart phone counter; Liberty SIM at Liberty stores ($10–$12, 4GB). One traveler noted: 'In front of the airport you can find a Walmart… you can buy a sim card for $1.' Another describes a genuine Claro activation at a legit reseller — multiple photos of passport + arrival stamp, slow but legit, ₡10,000 for 2 SIMs.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) BEFORE your flight install Airalo ($4.50–$9 for 1–3GB/week or $17 for 10GB/30 days at airalo.com) — activates instantly on landing, eliminates the airport-kiosk trap; (2) alternatives: Holafly, Nomad, Maya Mobile — all eSIMs work on Liberty/Claro/Kolbi networks; (3) if your phone isn't eSIM-capable, SKIP the SJO Claro kiosk — the real Kolbi store at Multiplaza Escazú (15-min Uber) or any in-city Walmart's in-store phone counter sells a legit ₡5,000–₡10,000 SIM with proper registration; (4) if you must use the airport kiosk: INSIST on a printed receipt (required under Costa Rica Ley 7472); PAY BY CARD (Claro officially accepts Visa/Mastercard; cash-only is the scam signal); test the SIM with a WhatsApp message before leaving; (5) if scammed: screenshot the transaction; file at consumidor.go.cr (Ley 7472 violation) + SUTEL telecom regulator + credit-card chargeback; (6) SJO offers free Wi-Fi ('Free-Wifi-AeropuertoSJO') — you can coordinate your Uber/shuttle without buying a SIM at all. How to avoid: Pre-install Airalo eSIM ($4.50–$17) BEFORE flight — skips the airport kiosk entirely. If SIM is required: wait and buy at Multiplaza Escazú Kolbi store or Walmart phone counter. At airport kiosk: demand printed receipt + pay only by Visa/Mastercard. Test SIM with WhatsApp message before leaving the kiosk — catches dead SIMs immediately. If scammed: file at consumidor.go.cr + SUTEL + credit-card chargeback (Ley 7472).

Scam alert in San Jose, Costa Rica — SJO Rental-Car Counter 'Mandatory Insurance' $2,000 Ambush — Expedia / Hertz / Fox Trap (accommodation, severity: high). This is the single highest-volume complaint in Costa Rica travel communities 2024–2026. A March 2025 traveler report: the traveler bought 'FULL coverage insurance from Expedia' and paid ~$1,000 for 3 weeks; on arrival at the offsite lot was told either accept a $2,032 mandatory local insurance OR pay a $32,000 USD deposit with 20% deducted for any damage; when the traveler refused they were 'left on the side of the road with 5 suitcases.' A top reply: 'Adobe and Vamos come out on top every time, and warnings about not booking through third party sites like Expedia.' Another: 'Even had this happen with Hertz.' Another: 'Same situation with me and Expedia and Fox Rental. Would not accept the Expedia insurance.' A November 2025 traveler report surfaces the legal reality, confirmed by another commenter: 'The law says the only required insurance is third-party liability (SLI/TPL)… NOT REQUIRED is any collision damage coverage.' TPL in 2025/2026 runs ~$13–$20/day — anything above is optional. The scam runs two ways: (1) Expedia/Priceline/Kayak's advertised $19/day balloons at the counter with $25–$40/day mandatory insurance + $2,000 deposit hold — third-party CDWs routinely rejected; (2) Hertz/Fox/Budget/National SJO counters stack 'Super CDW' to push $29/day to $90/day. Another traveler: 'If you decline CDW, you're required to bring proof of insurance from your credit card… don't forget the deposit — $2,000 for most rental companies.' Another: 'Vamos and Adobe seem to be much more straightforward about using rental insurance from a credit card.' Another: '$700 for 10 day rental with Adobe including all insurance — they were amazing.'

For travelers 2025/2026: (1) DO NOT BOOK via Expedia, Priceline, Kayak, Hotwire, Travelocity — book DIRECT with Adobe (adobecar.com), Vamos (vamosrentacar.com), or Wildrider; online quotes include TPL and are transparent; (2) if using Hertz/Budget/National, email the CR counter for an all-in written quote before landing, and bring your credit-card's rental-coverage letter (Amex Premium, Chase Sapphire Reserve Primary, Capital One Venture X Primary) on bank letterhead — required to decline CDW legally; (3) CR requires TPL (~$13–$20/day) — accept it; above is optional unless your card doesn't cover CR (most do); (4) expect $1,500–$3,000 deposit hold clearing 7–14 days post-return; (5) PHOTOGRAPH every panel on pickup + return (video walk-around) — 'pre-existing damage' counter-scam runs often; (6) Adobe, Vamos, Alamo have ZERO counter-shakedowns reported 2024–2026; Hertz/Fox/Budget/Expedia have the worst profile; (7) file disputes at consumidor.go.cr + Amex/Visa chargeback. How to avoid: Book DIRECT with Adobe, Vamos, or Wildrider — published all-in pricing, honored at counter. If using Hertz/Budget/National: email counter for written quote including TPL before landing. Bring printed credit-card CDW coverage letter (Amex Premium, Chase Sapphire Reserve Primary). Accept mandatory TPL only (~$13–$20/day) — decline CDW/Super CDW with written proof. Video walk-around on pickup + return; dispute via consumidor.go.cr + chargeback if ambushed.

Scam alert in San Jose, Costa Rica — Coca-Cola Bus Terminal Pickpocket & Luggage-Theft at the Zona Roja Edge (pickpocket, severity: high). Every Western government advisory flags one zone of San José specifically: the Coca-Cola bus terminal and the 'zona roja' north of the Mercado Central. Canada's travel advisory (travel.gc.ca, 2025): 'Specific trouble spots include downtown San José areas near the Coca-Cola bus terminal, central market, and public parks.' Australia's Smartraveller: 'petty crime is common near the central bus terminal in the Coca Cola… most likely on weekends.' The zone is dense, unlit, and the hub for nearly every long-distance bus (Tracopa SJO→Jacó/Quepos; Alfaro SJO→Montezuma; MEPE SJO→Puerto Viejo; Empresarios Unidos SJO→Puntarenas). A canonical Tracopa-bus case, documented in a March 2024 traveler thread, describes how thieves planted as passengers wait for a rest stop, strip the bus of laptops/phones/passports from overhead bins, and vanish into a waiting car; one female passenger lost her laptop. An October 2024 traveler thread collects the urban variants: 'Watch out for motorcyclists who can drive by and snatch a phone from your hand, or a necklace from your neck.' Another traveler thread warns: 'Plaza de la Cultura is safe during DAYLIGHT — pickpockets work the crowd.' For travelers 2025/2026: (1) AVOID Coca-Cola if possible — use Interbus (interbusonline.com) or Gray Line private shuttles ($49–$65 pp door-to-door, no terminal); (2) if using Tracopa/Alfaro/MEPE, arrive 15 minutes max ahead, stay inside the ticket office with bags on your lap, never accept 'help' with luggage from anyone not in company uniform; (3) SKIP Mercado Central and zona roja blocks north of Hotel Del Rey after dark; (4) on long-distance buses, never leave valuables in the overhead rack at a rest stop — daypack WITH you every time; (5) money belt for passport + 80% cash; decoy wallet in front pocket with expired card + ₡5,000; (6) phone on wrist-strap or zipped crossbody (Pacsafe); motorcycle-grab-from-stoplight is documented; (7) report at the Tourist Police Operations Center (San José hub opened 2025, English line) or OIJ 800-8000-645 within 24h. How to avoid: Skip Coca-Cola: book Interbus/Gray Line private shuttle ($49–$65 pp, door-to-door). Never leave valuables in overhead bin during bus rest stops — carry daypack every time. Money belt under clothing for passport + 80% cash; decoy wallet in front pocket. Avoid Mercado Central / zona roja after dark; daylight only, nothing valuable in pockets. Tourist Police 24/7 hub (2025) + OIJ 800-8000-645 within 24h for insurance claim.

Scam alert in San Jose, Costa Rica — Parque Central / Avenida 2 Cambista Currency-Exchange & 'Counterfeit Bill' Swap (financial-fraud, severity: moderate). Costa Rica has official casas de cambio and banks with BCCR (Banco Central de Costa Rica) rates ~₡515–₡530 per USD through 2025/2026 (~2% buy/sell spread). In Parque Central, Avenida 2 pedestrian strip, and around Plaza de la Cultura, informal cambistas (money-changers) approach tourists with whispered 'cambio, cambio?' and a fan of colones. Three scams run. First, the rate gouge — the quoted rate is 10–20% below market (₡450 per USD) and the cambista talks fast to close before the tourist pulls out xe.com. Second, the counterfeit-bill swap — the cambista takes your $100 USD, fans out ₡50,000 in real colones, palms one ₡20,000 out during the count and replaces it with a crisp counterfeit that feels plastic-smooth. A 2024 traveler report documents 'two dudes tried to scam me in San José' with a 'cambio del falso premio de lotería y otros timos callejeros' — the classic fake-lottery-prize + money-switch combo. Third, the snatch-and-run — the cambista 'counts,' feigns a mistake, asks for the dollars back, hands them to an accomplice instead of the tourist, and both vanish. Tico Times 'Costa Rica Expat Living: My Encounter with Money Changers' (June 2023) describes the pattern explicitly. A 2025 community traveler advises: 'pay in colones (and beware of the "this bill is counterfeit" scam)' — drivers claim the ₡20,000 you handed is fake, pocket yours, hand back a prepared counterfeit, demand replacement. Another 2024 community traveler: 'Biggest scam is exchanging your money at the airport. The conversion rate is terrible. Just go to a major bank.' BCCR ATMs and Banco Nacional / BAC / Scotiabank / BCR branches post rates within 1% of market.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) NEVER change money on the street — every whispered 'cambio' approach is a scam; (2) change at a bank branch with your passport, or withdraw colones from an in-branch ATM at a 1% spread; (3) pay shops, restaurants, taxis in COLONES not USD — removes the 'rounding' gouge; (4) check every ₡20,000 note: Carlos Luis Fallas watermark, a color-shifting security thread that flips green/blue when tilted, raised-print feel — counterfeits are smooth, lack the thread, don't flip colors; (5) if a cambista or driver claims your ₡20,000 is 'fake,' refuse to take it back and demand YOUR ORIGINAL visible in their hand — photograph it and call 911; the swap IS the scam; (6) use a no-FTF credit card (Capital One Venture, Chase Sapphire, Amex Platinum) for hotel + restaurants; colones cash only for taxis, tips, vendors; (7) BCCR ATM foreign-card limit ₡400,000/day (~$770); keep 3+ days of cash; (8) report at the San José Tourist Police Operations Center (2025) or OIJ 800-8000-645. How to avoid: Never change money on the street — only bank branches or in-branch ATMs. Check ₡20,000 for Carlos Luis Fallas watermark + color-shift security thread. Refuse 'your bill is counterfeit' swap — keep YOUR original note visible + photograph it. Pay shops/taxis in COLONES (not USD) — removes the rounding-up gouge. Credit card (no-FTF Capital One/Chase/Amex) for hotels/restaurants; report at OIJ 800-8000-645.

Scam alert in San Miguel de Allende, Mexico — SMA Luxury Hotel & Boutique Airbnb Fake-Luxury Fraud (tourist-trap, severity: high). Scam alert in Tamarindo, Costa Rica — Tamarindo Banco Nacional / BAC ATM Skimming + Counterfeit-Bill Swap (financial-fraud, severity: moderate). How to avoid: Use ATMs INSIDE bank branches during business hours (Scotiabank, BAC, BCR) — avoid curb units. Always withdraw colones not USD — decline DCC; saves 5–9% on every pull. Inspect every ₡20,000 note for Carlos Luis Fallas watermark + color-shift thread. Bring only pristine post-2013 USD bills; carry a credit card (Capital One, Chase, Amex) for restaurants. If skimmed: call bank within 30 min, file at Tamarindo Fuerza Pública + OIJ 800-8000-645.

For travelers in 2025/2026: (1) never accept a drink from a stranger already at the bar — buy your own and watch it poured; use Nightcap / SipChip test strips ($12 Amazon) if uncertain; (2) if you meet someone who needs 'somewhere to stay,' decline and book them an Uber home — as one traveler put it, 'if you aren't into it send her home in an Uber'; (3) if pressed for $500 next morning, refuse, pack, leave; call 911 not pay — pimp threats are usually bluffs; (4) Costa Rican hotels require cédula (ID) for every overnight guest (per traveler reports) — a partner who won't show cédula is a red flag; (5) at the casino, cash the bare minimum chips you're willing to lose; never walk to the ATM drunk — use the in-hotel ATM at Diria under camera; (6) the unlit beach path between Monkey Bar and Langosta is a documented mugging corridor — take an Uber or walk the main road; (7) emergency: 911, US Embassy 2519-2000, Tamarindo Fuerza Pública — file drink-spiking WITHIN 6 HOURS (toxicology window). How to avoid: Buy and watch your own drinks; carry Nightcap/SipChip test strips if uncertain. Anyone asking to stay the night — Uber them home; decline and still enjoy the date earlier next day. Demand cédula at any hotel check-in; a refusal = leave; Costa Rican law requires it. If extorted for $500: refuse, pack, call 911 + US Embassy 2519-2000 — don't pay. Drink-spiking: file at Fuerza Pública within 6h for toxicology + OIJ + travel-insurance claim.

Scam alert in Tulum, Mexico — Tulum Ruins 'Conservation Fee' & Mandatory Guide Scam (tourist-trap, severity: high). Tulum Archaeological Zone is Mexico's most-visited Caribbean-coast Mayan ruins — and hosts a 2025 'conservation fee' + 'mandatory guide' scam ecosystem. Multiple 2025 traveler reports document this pattern, including first-person accounts of the 'Tulum Tax Scam,' the cross-site 'Conservation Fee Scam' in Cancún, 2025 fee controversy covering Tulum and Akumal, and adjacent warnings about Chichen Itzá tour scams. Legitimate costs: Tulum ruins entry is MX$100 (INAH federal). NO additional 'conservation fee' exists. Optional licensed guides charge MX$800–$1,200 PER GROUP (4–8 people), not per person. Parking at OFFICIAL lot is MX$150. The 2025 scams: (a) 'ecological conservation fee MX$500 per person' demanded at gate by touts in uniforms — fake; (b) 'mandatory Mayan guide MX$600 per person' at entrance — NO guide required; self-guided maps free; (c) ticket-seller imposters 200m before gate selling 'combined ticket MX$800' — no combo exists; (d) 'parking fee MX$500' at unofficial lots (real MX$150); (e) 'cenote + ruins combo MX$2,000 per person' bundled with commission-stop lunch; (f) 'photo package MX$400' upsell at the Castillo viewpoint; (g) 'mandatory donation to Mayan community MX$200' post-visit. For older travelers: (1) buy Tulum ruins entry at the OFFICIAL INAH ticket window — MX$100 per foreigner; no additional fees; (2) park ONLY at the OFFICIAL lot MX$150 with government-issued receipt; ignore 'unofficial' touts directing elsewhere; (3) NO mandatory guide — self-guide with free INAH map; optional licensed guides are MX$800–$1,200 PER GROUP (verify license badge with photo + number); (4) REFUSE every 'conservation fee', 'Mayan community donation', 'photo package' demand; (5) arrive at 8 AM opening — by 10 AM tour buses flood the site; (6) wear comfortable walking shoes, hat, sun protection; the site is exposed and hot 35°C+ summer; (7) for swimming at the adjacent beach, walk down from the ruins — beach access is MX$50 if via the site; (8) traveler reports have specific tout-location warnings to memorise. How to avoid: Pay ONLY MX$100 at official INAH ticket window; no extra fees Park at OFFICIAL lot MX$150 with government receipt NO mandatory guide; optional MX$800–$1,200 PER GROUP REFUSE every 'conservation fee', 'donation', 'photo package' demand Arrive 8 AM opening before tour-bus flood

Scam alert in Tulum, Mexico — Tulum Beach Zone 'Hotel Zone' Restaurant Bill-Padding & Beach Club Upcharge (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Tulum's 'Zona Hotelera' (Beach Zone, 6 km south of Downtown Tulum) hosts Mexico's most-infamous 2025 restaurant-bill padding ecosystem. Traveler reports document the pattern, including first-person 2025 accounts and the surcharge controversy covering Tulum and Akumal. The 2025 scams: (a) Beach Road restaurants with USD-only menus at 2–3x Mexico norms (US$18 for breakfast, US$35+ for mains); (b) 'service charge 18%' pre-added + tip line (double-tipping trap); (c) credit-card surcharge 10–18% added unannounced; (d) 'environmental fee MX$150 per person' surcharge at some beach restaurants (fake); (e) Beach Club 'entry minimum US$50 per person food/drink' + 'VIP bed US$200' that's an uncovered wooden platform; (f) 'bottle minimum US$300+' at trendy beach clubs (Papaya Playa, Nomade) — one bottle of mid-shelf tequila US$400; (g) 'photo package US$100' upsells from Beach Road nightclubs; (h) 'cash only' smaller restaurants with 'no receipt' policy (chargeback-proof); (i) bill switcheroo where itemised receipt ≠ card charge. For older travelers: (1) eat in DOWNTOWN TULUM (not Beach Zone) — restaurants on Av. Tulum and Av. Satélite have authentic Yucatec food at 1/3 Beach Zone prices; reputable: Charly's Vegan Tacos, Antojitos La Chiapaneca, El Tacoqueto; (2) if you DO go to Beach Zone, budget US$60–$100 per person for a meal regardless of 'deals'; (3) INSPECT the bill line-by-line; refuse 'environmental fee', 'service charge + tip' double-dipping, and 10–18% card surcharges; (4) for Beach Clubs, confirm the MINIMUM + any 'VIP' charge BEFORE sitting; photograph the menu; (5) REFUSE 'bottle minimum' — order drinks individually off the menu; (6) USD menus usually pad the exchange by 10–15% — ask for MX$ bill; (7) traveler reports note the region has higher legitimate VAT (IVA 16%) but it should be in menu prices not added on; (8) bring a calculator and verify totals; (9) pay with credit card (chargeback leverage) not cash where possible. How to avoid: Eat in DOWNTOWN TULUM (Av. Tulum/Satélite): 1/3 Beach Zone prices Reputable: Charly's Vegan Tacos, Antojitos La Chiapaneca, El Tacoqueto Inspect bill; refuse 'service + tip' double; card surcharge 0–3% Beach Club: confirm minimum + VIP charge BEFORE sitting Request MX$ bill (not USD which pads 10–15% exchange)

Scam alert in Tulum, Mexico — Tulum Cenote Tour Unlicensed Operator & Fake 'Private Access' (tourist-trap, severity: high). Tulum is surrounded by world-class cenotes (Dos Ojos, Gran Cenote, Cenote Calavera, Casa Cenote) and the tour ecosystem hosts a 2025 unlicensed-operator + entry-fee overcharge pattern. Multiple 2025 community discussions cover cenote tour scams, cross-region cenote guidance, and documented 2025 traveler experiences. Legitimate costs: Gran Cenote entry MX$500, Cenote Dos Ojos MX$350, Cenote Calavera MX$250, Cenote Cristal MX$250, Casa Cenote MX$150. Reputable small-group tour (3–4 cenotes + transport + lunch) MX$1,500–$2,500 per person. The 2025 scams: (a) Downtown Tulum tour booths selling 'private cenote access MX$3,500 per person' when public entry is MX$250–$500; (b) 'VIP guide + underwater photo package' bundle MX$5,000 (photos rarely delivered); (c) fake 'mandatory Mayan shaman cleansing MX$800' at cenote entry; (d) unlicensed tour operators without life jackets, insurance, or SEMARNAT permits; (e) 'exclusive Dos Ojos underwater cave dive MX$8,000' for non-certified visitors (cave diving requires full cave certification — this is either fraud or dangerous); (f) 'commission restaurant' added to tour route; (g) 'life-jacket rental MX$200' at cenotes where jackets are INCLUDED in entry; (h) rental-car drivers directed to 'better cenote' by hotel concierge (commission shop). For older travelers: (1) drive yourself (rental car or Uber day-hire) to cenote entries — Dos Ojos MX$350, Gran Cenote MX$500, Cenote Calavera MX$250 — pay official ticket window; (2) book guided tours ONLY via Google 4.7+ operators: Jugo Cenote Experiences, Mex-On Adventures, Yuchitur — MX$1,500–$2,500 per person for 3-cenote day; (3) REFUSE every 'private cenote access', 'Mayan shaman', 'VIP guide package' upsell; (4) for Dos Ojos, accept ONLY open-water snorkel (not cave dive unless fully cave-certified with your own instructor); (5) bring biodegradable sunscreen ONLY (chemical sunscreens damage cenote ecosystems — some sites require rinse-off); (6) older-traveler-friendly cenotes: Casa Cenote (easy shore entry), Cenote Cristal (walkway + platform); (7) avoid Gran Cenote 11 AM–3 PM (tour-bus flood); (8) 2–3 cenotes in one day is enough; 4+ is exhausting for older travelers. How to avoid: Pay at official cenote windows: Dos Ojos MX$350, Gran MX$500 Tours via Jugo Cenote, Mex-On, Yuchitur (Google 4.7+) REFUSE 'private access', 'shaman', 'VIP package' upsells NO cave dive unless fully cave-certified with own instructor Biodegradable sunscreen only; 2–3 cenotes max per day

Scam alert in Tulum, Mexico — Tulum 'Eco-Luxury' Hotel Zone Airbnb & Booking Fraud (tourist-trap, severity: high). Tulum's rapid 'eco-luxury' boom 2020–2025 has outpaced legitimate accommodation supply, creating a 2025 fake-listing + price-gouging ecosystem. Traveler reports document 2025 patterns and establish baselines. The 2025 scams: (a) fake Airbnb 'eco-luxury jungle cabaña' listings using stolen photos — properties don't exist or are 200m inland (not 'beachfront'); (b) Instagram DM/WhatsApp 'exclusive private villa rental' at US$400/night requiring full upfront payment via bank transfer; (c) Facebook 'Tulum Luxury Villas' groups with fake profiles — pattern identical to Seminyak Bali villa scams; (d) confirmed-booking cancellations during high season (Dec–Mar, July–Aug) with re-listing at 3–5x rate; (e) on-arrival bait-and-switch to inferior properties; (f) 'cleaning deposit US$150' cash that never returns; (g) 'no-electricity, bio-toilet only' surprises pitched as 'eco-authentic' when really just power failures; (h) 'mandatory gratuity 15–20%' added at beach-road 'managed' cabañas that's pocketed by middlemen. For older travelers: (1) book Tulum accommodations ONLY via Booking.com, Hotels.com, Expedia (platform-protected); OR direct from verified hotel websites (Be Tulum, Papaya Playa Project, Nomade, La Zebra) — all with Booking.com 4.7+ ratings; (2) AVOID Instagram DM, WhatsApp-only, Facebook group, and small-time 'villa manager' listings; (3) NEVER bank-transfer to private sellers — platform secure payment only; (4) for peak season (Dec–Mar, July–Aug), book 4–6 months ahead on Booking.com with free cancellation; (5) AVOID Airbnb for peak season on Tulum — cancellation pattern is documented; (6) confirm BEACH access in writing ('beachfront' vs '2-minute walk to beach' are very different) — some eco-cabañas are actually 200–500m inland; (7) confirm POWER, AC, WIFI status in writing — some 'eco' properties have only generator power 3 hours/night; (8) for older travelers, prefer actual hotels over 'cabaña' concepts; (9) budget: Tulum Beach Zone is US$300–$1,500+ per night peak season; Downtown Tulum is US$60–$200 for far better value. How to avoid: Book ONLY via Booking.com, Hotels.com, Expedia (platform protection) AVOID Instagram DM, WhatsApp, Facebook group listings NEVER bank-transfer to private sellers Confirm BEACH, POWER, AC, WIFI status in writing Prefer Downtown Tulum US$60–$200 vs Beach Zone US$300+

Scam alert in Tulum, Mexico — Tulum Beach Zone Rental-Car Theft & 'Broken Meter' Parking Shakedown (transport, severity: high). Tulum Beach Road has a documented 2025 parking-enforcement + rental-car break-in ecosystem that mirrors the Playa del Carmen highway-checkpoint pattern. Traveler reports document the 'Police scam' pattern with first-person 2025 accounts and broader community baselines. The 2025 scams: (a) 'parking enforcement officer' (fake or real municipal) at Beach Road 'finding' infractions — MX$1,500–$5,000 cash demanded; (b) 'boot removal fee' at parking-restricted zones where your car has been 'booted' for 'wrong parking' — MX$2,000; (c) rental-car window smash-and-grab at unguarded beach parking (Sian Ka'an approach, Ruins Beach) while tourist is in the water; (d) 'parking attendant' demanding Rp 500–1,000 cash deposit with 'we watch your car' — then doesn't actually watch; (e) rental-car GPS-tracker theft where unattended car is stolen from Beach Road; (f) 'car damage during parking' fraud at return (same pattern as Isla/Holbox golf cart); (g) 'broken meter fee' ticket on windshield demanding MX$500 cash to pay at 'nearby' kiosk (fraud). For older travelers: (1) use Uber or taxi for Beach Zone visits — avoid rental car if possible; Tulum Beach Road has limited legitimate parking, and unattended rental cars are theft targets; (2) if driving, park ONLY at hotel valet (free for hotel guests) OR at pay-to-park lots with receipt; (3) NEVER leave anything visible in rental car — bags, phones, cameras must be in trunk or with you; (4) if 'parking enforcement' approaches, ask for BADGE + officer number and written ticket (NOT cash); (5) REFUSE 'boot removal fee' and 'broken meter' windshield tickets demanding cash — legitimate tickets are PAID at the treasury office with written stub; (6) for Sian Ka'an (1-hour drive), park at designated Muyil entry point with ranger station — not informal roadside pullouts; (7) rental-car theft requires police denuncia at Ministerio Público Tulum (+52 984 871 2109) within 24 hours for insurance claim; (8) bring sufficient rental insurance — Mexican third-party liability + comprehensive; (9) traveler reports have specific location warnings. How to avoid: Use Uber/taxi for Beach Zone; avoid rental-car parking If driving, hotel valet OR pay-to-park lot with receipt only NEVER leave anything visible in rental car REFUSE 'boot fee' and 'broken meter' windshield-ticket cash demands Tulum MP (+52 984 871 2109) for theft denuncia within 24 hours

Scam alert in Tulum, Mexico — Tulum Airport (TQO) 'Mandatory Tourism Tax' & Ticket Verification Scam (transport, severity: moderate). Tulum opened a new international airport (TQO) in December 2023 and hosts a 2025 departure-scam ecosystem mirroring Cancún's Visitax fraud. Traveler reports document the 'Tulum Tax Scam,' the cross-site 'Conservation Fee Scam' in Cancún, and 2025 posts bluntly titled 'DON'T PAY BULLSHIT EXIT-TAX!' covering the regional fraud. The 2025 scams: (a) 'Visitax verification agent' at TQO departure demanding US$30–$60 per person 'before you can board' — real Visitax is MX$271 paid ONLINE via visitax.gob.mx; (b) 'tourism tax processing fee' tablet-based phishing that clones credit cards; (c) 'luggage inspection fee' Rp 200–500 per bag demanded unofficially; (d) 'mandatory passport re-stamping fee US$15' — no such fee; (e) WhatsApp phishing texts claiming 'your Tulum departure tax is unpaid'; (f) 'skip the line US$25' upsell at immigration (no skip-line exists); (g) fake 'FMM return form fee' — the tourist-card return is free. For older travelers: (1) pay Visitax ONLY via visitax.gob.mx (official Quintana Roo government portal) BEFORE your trip — save PDF confirmation to phone; MX$271 per person ages 4+; (2) IGNORE every TQO 'tax agent' or 'processing fee' approach — the government does NOT collect tax at the airport; (3) the ONLY legitimate airport fees are ticket-price-inclusive airport taxes (shown on your boarding pass) and Visitax (paid online pre-trip); (4) NEVER hand your credit card at any airport 'tax payment' kiosk or tablet; (5) REFUSE every 'luggage inspection', 'passport re-stamping', 'FMM fee' demand — none is legitimate; (6) if pressured, show your visitax.gob.mx PDF and walk to the airline counter; (7) WhatsApp/SMS 'unpaid tax' texts are phishing — ignore, don't click links; (8) traveler reports have specific TQO-airport warnings; (9) US Embassy 24-hr +52 55 8526 2561 if escalated. How to avoid: Pay Visitax ONLY via visitax.gob.mx BEFORE trip (MX$271 pp) Save PDF confirmation; show if challenged IGNORE every TQO airport 'tax agent' approach NEVER hand card at any airport 'tax' kiosk or tablet Refuse 'luggage/passport/FMM' fee demands — none exist
